Materials and Methods

Site Description and Sample Collection

The Flint Hills region of the Great Plains in Northeast Kansas is a tallgrass prairie used primarily for cattle grazing and agriculture (O’Brien et al. 2007). Two streams were selected from each of three main land-use categories, agricultural, pristine, and urban, and their characteristics are given in Table 1. Kings Creek N4D, North Creek, and Campus Creek were sampled in 2003, with the others sampled in 2004. All analyses were performed near the time of sampling.

Sediment samples were collected cleanly at the start, midpoint, and end of each reach (125 to 300 m; O’Brien et al. 2007). Table 2 provides parameters related to stream N-cycle processes that were measured in conjunction with our study. Sediment samples were collected to a depth of 3-5 cm in ~250-ml Mason jars. Leaf litter and algal mat grab samples were collected haphazardly when observed along a reach. Algal mat samples were collected in 10-ml Vacutainer tubes. Samples for N_2-fixation assays were transported at ambient temperature and assays were begun in the laboratory within a few hours. Subsamples held for molecular analyses were placed in sterile containers, frozen immediately in the field, transported on dry ice, and stored at –80 °C prior to analysis.

Acetylene Reduction Assays of Nitrogen Fixation

The metal lids of the 250-ml jars used for sampling were fitted with rubber septa and sealed with silicone vacuum grease creating gas-tight vessels, the headspace of which were accessed by syringe. Jars were filled to approximately two-thirds with sediments that was covered in a layer (~1 cm) of stream water. Since nitrogenase is sensitive to oxygen, the jars were not left open to the air after collection and the small amount headspace oxygen was rapidly exhausted by microbes in the samples. Upon return to the laboratory, acetylene gas was injected into the headspace of the jars (to ~10% v/v). Algal samples were assayed in Vacutainer tubes. Samples with 2 to 6 replicates were incubated at room temperature in natural light and measurements were taken 1, 3, 7, and 14 d after collection. The weights of the sediment samples (~200 g) were recorded to express N_2 fixation per g sediment. The planar surface of the sediment sample in the Mason jar was similar to the area from which the sample was collected (diameter = 6 cm) and this was used to estimate N_2-fixation rates on an areal basis. Similar estimates were made for algal grab samples.

The conversion of acetylene to ethylene by nitrogenase is used as a surrogate for N_2 fixation (Jensen and Cox 1983). The ethylene content of aliquots (0.2 ml) of the headspace gas from the N_2-fixation assays were determined using the method of Reddy et al. (1993) by gas chromatography (Hewlett Packard 6890) with hydrogen flame ionization detection and a microbore DB5 column. Adjustments were made for the trace amount of ethylene found in the acetylene gas and a standard curve was generated by diluting commercial ethylene gas. We use a conversion factor of 3.8 acetylene molecules reduced per one dinitrogen molecule reduced (Jensen and Cox 1983). Theoretical ratios of 3:1 are often applied to N_2-fixation assays (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Grimm and Petrone 1997; Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh

</page>

<page number="3">

2006), but a 4:1 conversion ratio also has been used (Zehr and Montoya 2007; Kunza and Hall 2014).

Bivariate correlation analyses were performed in SPSS Statistics v23 (IBM) to derive Pearson coefficients through pairwise comparisons of measured processes, environmental conditions, stream parameters, and gene abundances. Numerical data were log-transformed for analysis, unless otherwise stated. Pearson correlations of \( p \leq 0.05 \) were considered to be statistically significant in the 2-tailed analyses routinely performed.

Direct Metagenomic DNA Extraction

DNA was directly extracted from sediment, leaf litter, and algal mat samples using the protocol of Bürgmann et al. (2001) with modifications as followed by Kilmer et al. (2014). Environmental samples (~0.5 g) were processed with a bead-beater and extracted with CTAB buffer, followed by phenol extraction and precipitation with polyethylene glycol before collection by centrifugation, washing, and resuspension in buffer. Purity was assessed spectrophotometrically (Genesys 5) by measuring \( A_{260}/A_{280} \) (DNA to protein) and \( A_{260}/A_{230} \) (DNA to humic acids) ratios.

Gene Counting by Real-time PCR

Real-time PCR was performed (Smart Cycler II; Cepheid Technology) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The reaction mixture contained (per 25 µL-reaction): SYBR Premix EX Taq (2x, TaKara), 12.5 µL; PCR forward and reverse primer (10 µM), 0.5 µL each; template DNA extract (≤400 ng), 2 µL; dH2O, 9.5 µL. The nifH gene primers were UNIFF19F (5′–GCIWTYTYAYGGIAARGGIGG–3′) and NifDN (3′–ADNGCCATCATYTCNCC–5′) generating a 464-bp amplicon (Zehr and McReynolds 1989; Ueda et al. 1995; Zehr et al. 1995). Real-time PCR amplification began with 60 s at 95 °C, followed by 45 cycles of 5 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 50 °C, and 15 s at 72 °C, and finally a hold at 72 °C for 60 s. Samples were assayed three to six times to determine typical deviations between different extracts of the same sample and from different amplifications of a single extract. A universal bacterial 16S rRNA gene primer set, EUB338 (5′–ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG–3′) and EUB518 (5′–ATTACCGCGGCTGG–3′), generated a ~200-bp amplicon with PCR as above with 40 s annealing at 53 °C (Fierer et al. 2005). Negative controls were sterile dH2O and a positive control, Cyanothecae sp. str. ATCC 51142 genomic DNA, was used to construct standard curves of gene copy number. The threshold value was 30 fluorescence units and C_t was calculated by the instrument. PCR products were confirmed using 2% agarose gel electrophoresis. Melting curves demonstrated high quality real-time PCR products.

Potential inhibition PCR by contaminants in DNA extracts was assessed using an exogenously added kanamycin-resistance gene from Pseudomonas fluorescens R8 Tn5 pho mutant M1 (Williams and Fletcher 1996) grown in LB media supplemented with 50 µg ml^{-1} kanamycin, as previously described (Caton et al. 2004b). Real-time PCR reactions (annealing at 63 °C) contained a known quantity of the kanamycin gene, aliquots (2 µl) of extracts, and the primers KanR: 5′–GCTGACGGAATTTATGCCTCTTC–3′; positions 572-594 and KanF: 5′–CACCATGAGTGACGACTGAATCC–3′; positions 224-246.

</page>

<page number="4">

Inhibition of PCR amplification was less than 2%, compared to control reactions with no added extract.

NifH Clone Libraries and Cladistics

NifH clone libraries were generated using a TOPO-TA blue-white cloning system in E. coli (Invitrogen). Ten separate amplicon populations were purified by band excision from a 2% agarose gels and pooled for each sample. Clones (~200) were randomly collected and inoculated into 96-well plates. Plasmid isolation and insert sequencing was performed by a commercial vendor (Agencourt) using the UNIFF19F/NifDN primer set. Sequences were trimmed to remove remaining vector regions, leaving reads of 191-278 bp for analysis. The 125 reliable sequences obtained were too short for inclusion as a group in GenBank, but are available from the permanent SOAR repository at Wichita State University (https://soar.wichita.edu/handle/10057/14382).

Sequences were aligned using Clustal-W and trimmed in MacClade v4.08 (Sinauer Associates). Contextual 16S rRNA gene sequences were identified in GenBank using BLAST or by comparison to relevant literature (Ueda et al. 1995). Sequences were trimmed to equal lengths and positions with gaps and ambiguous bases were ignored, giving 191 positions for analysis. PAUP 4.0 b10 generated phylogenetic trees using distance analysis with Jukes-Cantor rules and the neighbor-joining algorithm. The tree was rooted using the sequence from Methanocaldococcus jannaschii as the functional outgroup. The diversity of nifH genes and species assignments between and within the three stream types were compared using MEGA7 (Kumar et al. 2016), the Biodiversity Assessment Tools (BAT) package function beta.multi within R (Cardoso et al. 2014), and log-likelihood ratio tests using the \( G \) statistic and two-sample ranking with the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (Zar 2009).

Results

Rates of Nitrogen Fixation

The results of N\(_2\) fixation assays are presented in Table 3 for stream sediment samples taken from three locations along each of six prairie stream reaches. The highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation in stream sediments were observed at locations on two reaches of Kings Creek, the least impacted stream, having the lowest nitrate levels in our study (Table 3). Although it is considered an agricultural stream, Natalie’s Creek had nitrate levels as low as the pristine stream Kings Creek at the time of sampling; however, it did not exhibit high N\(_2\)-fixation rates in sediments. The North Creek agricultural stream sediment had somewhat elevated nitrate levels and a high rate of N\(_2\) fixation was observed in some sediment samples. The lowest rates of N\(_2\) fixation were observed in the urban stream sediments and these corresponded to the greatest chronic nitrate loads. It should be noted that acetylene reduction assays are surrogates for N fixation and a common conversion factor (3.8) was used here for calculations (Jensen and Cox 1983). While this allows for comparison within these data, actual values for N fixation would be altered if this ratio were to differ substantially between samples. Stable isotope methods would give a direct measure of N fixation activity that could be used to determine if any samples deviated from the common ratio used for

</page>

<page number="5">

conversion, however, the accepted range is 3 to 4 (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Zehr and Montoya 2007).

The rates of N_2 fixation across our six prairie streams varied between 1.6 and 28.0 fmol g^{-1} h^{-1}. The highest rates were observed in pristine prairie streams and the lowest rates were observed in urban stream sediments (Fig. 1). Log-transformed rates and concentrations (n = 6, fd = 4) were used for statistical analyses using Pearson correlations. N_2-fixation rates were significantly negatively correlated (r = -0.811, p = 0.050) with the extent of chronic N loading of the streams, as measured by NO_3^- levels in sediments. In a similar fashion, DIN levels in the streams were negatively correlated with N_2-fixation activity in sediments, with marginal statistical significance (r = -0.745, p = 0.089) (Fig. 2). This is expected since nearly all of the DIN was due to NO_3^- (Table 2), with NO_3^- and DIN levels significantly positively correlated (r = 0.969, p = 0.001). Rates of N_2 fixation were not correlated with NH_4-N (r = -0.181, p = 0.731) or with DON (r = 0.691, p = 0.196).

Overall rates of denitrification were low and varied from undetectable to 44.0 μg N m^{-2} s^{-1} (Fig. 3). Denitrification rates in sediments were significantly negatively correlated with N_2-fixation activity (r = -0.809, p = 0.050). The rates of nitrification were not significantly correlated to the rates of N_2 fixation (r = -0.616, p = 0.193), nor were NO_3^- fluxes (r = -0.548, p = 0.260).

Significant correlations were not observed between N_2-fixation rates and PAR (r = -0.334, p = 0.517) or GPP (r = 0.331, p = 0.522). No significant correlation (r = 0.446, p = 0.376) was found between N_2-fixation rates and DO either. The width (r = 0.047, p = 0.929) or depth (r = 0.125, p = 0.814) of the streams did not significantly correlate with N_2-fixation rates. A marginally significant negative correlation (r = -0.799, p = 0.057) was observed between temperature and N_2-fixation rates across our six streams. Stream type significantly correlated (r = 0.923, p = 0.009) with N_2-fixation rates as expected, since the streams had different levels of chronic N loading.

In addition to regular sediment sampling along each reach, targeted grab samples were taken of leaf litter and algal mats along these reaches (Table 4). Rates of N_2 fixation in these targeted grab samples were generally higher than in sediment samples. Leaf litter samples from Kings Creek exhibited high rates of N_2 fixation in the N4D reach. Natalie’s Creek had algal mats along its banks and these exhibited very high rates of N_2 fixation. Similarly, the algal materials from the Big Blue River Ditch also exhibited high rates of N_2 fixation. The Big Blue River Ditch is canalized in this region and the algal samples were taken from depressions in the concrete and from algal streamers.

Levels of *NifH* Genes

Direct DNA extracts were made from field-frozen sediment samples taken at the same locations as those assayed for N_2-fixation activity. The greatest overall abundance of *nifH* genes was observed in the sediments from Kings Creek, with all samples above 10^4 copies g^{-1} (Table 3). Campus Creek, an urban stream, had relatively high *nifH* abundance overall. One sample from Natalie’s Creek also showed high *nifH* abundance. The abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes varied from 10^8 to 10^{11} copies g^{-1} sediment. There was a

<page number="6">

significant correlation (r = 0.941, \( p = 0.005 \)) between stream type and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance, but there was not a significant correlation (r = 0.588, \( p = 0.219 \)) between stream type and \( nifH \) gene abundance. Chronic NO\(_3^-\) loads were marginally correlated with bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.756, \( p = 0.082 \)), while \( nifH \) gene abundance was not (r = 0.472, \( p = 0.345 \)).

There was not a direct correlation between \( nifH \) gene abundance and N\(_2\)-fixation rates (r = 0.295, \( p = 0.570 \)) when comparing six stream averages or when comparing data for each reach (n = 17, r = 0.381, \( p = 0.131 \)). The abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes was positively correlated (r = 0.830, \( p = 0.041 \)) with N\(_2\)-fixation rates, while \( nifH \) gene abundance was only marginally correlated (r = 0.704, \( p = 0.118 \)) with N\(_2\)-fixation rates. No significant correlations were found between \( nifH \) or bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundances with DON, DIN, width, depth, PAR, GPP, DO, nitrate flux, denitrification, or nitrification. NH\(_4\)-N negatively correlates (r = 0.970, \( p = 0.006 \)) with \( nifH \) gene abundance, but not bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.485, \( p = 0.407 \)). There was a significant negative correlation between stream temperature and both \( nifH \) gene abundance (r = 0.869, \( p = 0.025 \)) and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.899, \( p = 0.015 \)).

Targeted grab samples of leaf litter and algal mats mainly gave high abundances of \( nifH \) genes (Table 4), similar to the highest values obtained from sediment samples. Small sample size from the canalized concrete bed of Big Blue River Ditch may have led to the low values obtained from two small samples there. No significant correlations were observed between N\(_2\)-fixation rates, stream type, and \( nifH \) gene abundance for the grab samples. While the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation generally were observed in grab samples, this was not correlated with \( nifH \) gene abundances.

**NifH Gene Clone Libraries**

Clone libraries were made from pooled PCR amplicons derived from metagenomic extracts of stream sediment samples. Clones of \( nifH \) genes from each of these libraries (125 total clones sequenced) were compared, along with contextual sequences, to generate the summary phylogenetic tree shown in Fig. 4. A complete tree is presented in supporting materials (Fig. S1). *NifH* genes from members of the *Deltaproteobacteria* were detected in the sediments of all three stream types, as were *nifH* genes from *Bradyrhizobium, Methylomonas, Rhizobium*, and *Sinorhizobium*. Cyanobacterial *nifH* sequences were observed in the agricultural and urban streams, although sediments and not algal mats were sampled. Quite a number of groups of *nifH* sequences that only cluster with sequences from uncultured organisms were observed in each of the streams. These include clones from grass, oil field, and rice soils, Mangrove rhizosphere, and marine environments. The larger cluster near *Bradyrhizobium japonicum* did not have strong matches to known sequences. No sequences related to *Archaea, Azotobacter, Chlorobium, Klebsiella*, or *Rhodobacter* were detected.

Taxonomic assignments were made from *nifH* sequences and compared across streams, showing obvious differences in guild composition. For example, *Methylococcus* sequences were only observed in the agricultural stream and sequences related to an uncultured Mangrove soil *nifH* were found in high abundance only in the urban stream. When isolates

</page>

<page number="7">

are binned at higher taxonomic levels (Cyanobacteria, *Deltaproteobacteria*, Others, Rhizobia, and Unknowns) the *G* statistic can be applied. Diazotroph communities among streams significantly differed by stream type by this measure (fd = 4, *p* <0.001). Whether binning *nifH* taxons by clade or higher levels, Wilcoxon rank sum analysis supported the hypothesis that diazotroph guild composition varies significantly with stream type (n = 5 to 14, *p* <0.01 to <0.001). When *nifH* sequences were examined directly, without assigning taxon and making common evolutionary assumptions (Jukes-Cantor rules), the results were quite different (Table 5). Within-group and between-group mean genetic distances were similar and generally high (>1). Net between group mean distances were low, taken together, indicating that diversity within each group was similar to diversity between the groups. This was supported by beta diversity analyses using Jaccard coefficients where values were consistently high (approaching 1) and were insensitive to randomization between groups. The coefficient of differentiation was very low (0.089 on a scale of 0 to 1), suggesting that the populations of *nifH* genes among the streams have similarities because there is substantial gene flow between these communities.

Discussion

The overall rates of N$_2$ fixation observed for prairie stream sediments in the current report are of the same magnitude as fixation rates from previous studies of small streams (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Leland and Carter 1985; Francis et al. 1985, Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007). The metanalysis of Marcarelli et al. (2008) reported that the mean N$_2$-fixation rate among 22 streams was approximately 1 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, with a high of 30 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. Nitrogen-fixation activity in the stream sediments of our study ranged from about 0.1 to 3.0 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. Rates of N$_2$ fixation were higher in grab samples suggesting that leaf litter and algal biofilms are important contributors to whole-stream N$_2$-fixation activity.

There was a significant correlation between N$_2$-fixation rates and levels of chronic N loading in these small streams (as NO$_3^-$ or DIN). It is well known that nitrate can inhibit N$_2$-fixation activity and this also has been observed in streams (Capone and Carpenter 1982; Grimm 1994). However, in brackish marshes, N$_2$ fixation proceeded even with the addition of fixed N compounds (Piceno and Lovell 2000). Controls on the rate of N$_2$ fixation appear more complicated than simply a response to NO$_3^-$ levels. Temperature was found to be correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates in our streams, as observed previously (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Grimm and Petrone 1997). Light and productivity (PAR and GPP) however were not correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. Phosphorus levels were not measured as part of the LINXII project. Denitrification rates were significantly correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. This was expected since denitrification rates also appear to vary with nitrate levels (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2006, 2007), although this correlation was not strong in the current study (r = 0.695, *p* = 0.126).

The rates of NO$_3^-$ uptake in our streams ranged from 0.24 to 15.4 mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, in North Creek and Campus Creek, respectively (O’Brien et al. 2007). Highly impacted urban streams exhibited uptake rates of >5 mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, while pristine and agricultural streams exhibited uptake rates of \( \leq 1 \) mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. While NO$_3^-$ uptake rates were higher than N$_2$-

</page>

<page number="8">

fixation rates for all streams, those with lower uptake rates tended to have higher fixation rates (r = 0.685, \( p = 0.133 \)). For the pristine prairie stream Kings K2A, the rate of N\(_2\) fixation is about 15% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate (on an areal basis). This suggests that N\(_2\) fixation can be a significant contributor to stream N budgets. However, for our other pristine prairie stream Kings N4D, the N\(_2\)-fixation rate was only 2% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate. None of the other streams had N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were more than 6% of their NO\(_3^-\) uptake rates, with the Big Blue Ditch value being only 0.02%. Taken together, this suggests that the impact of N\(_2\) fixation to the N budget of small streams is variable. While N\(_2\) fixation may be a substantial contributor in streams with low chronic N loads, this does not appear to be consistent, and N\(_2\) fixation does not seem to be a substantial contributor to N budgets in small streams with higher chronic N loads. This is in agreement with previous studies, both in terms of the variability observed across streams, but also in concluding that N\(_2\) fixation can be important in certain oligotrophic streams and perhaps only at certain times (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007; Marcarelli et al. 2008; Scott et al. 2009; Lang et al. 2012; Kunza and Hall 2013, 2014).

Patchiness is a key feature of small streams, in terms of leaf litter and algal mat distributions, and this reflects differences in N\(_2\)-fixation rates across stream compartments. The highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation are often associated with patches of leaf litter and algal mats, and the current study agrees (Henry and Fisher 2003; Marcarelli et al. 2008). Targeted grab samples in our study exhibited the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation, substantially higher than equivalent amounts of sediments. To better understand the role of N\(_2\) fixation in stream N budgets, coverage estimates for algal mats and leaf litter are needed, but this was not done rigorously in the current study. No significant correlations were observed between N\(_2\)-fixation rates and estimates of fine benthic organic matter or ash-free dry mass (g dry mass m\(^{-2}\)) of leaves, wood, and epilithon (estimates from O’Brien et al. 2007). Samples of algal mats exhibited N\(_2\)-fixation rates some 30-fold greater than in the bottom sediments. Thus, even if only 3% of a basin was covered with algal mats, their contribution to N\(_2\) fixation might equal that of the remaining 97% of the basin comprised of sediments.

At Kings Creek N4D, patches of leaf litter were found to have N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were 4-fold greater than the sediments of this reach. This stream has a cobbled bottom with limited areas of sediment. Seasonal factors and scouring events will have a role in determining the balance between fixation in sediments and leaf litter in streams like Kings Creek. Finally, the concrete basin of Big Blue River Ditch had remarkably productive patches. N\(_2\)-fixation activity was high in algal communities within depressions and grooves in the concrete and in algal streamers attached to the bottom. The patchiness of organisms actively fixing N make whole-stream assessments more difficult especially since the patches are often transient and subject to changes in stream flow, seasons, and nutrient inputs.

The contribution of N\(_2\) fixation to stream N budgets may be more significant in specific patches of streams or in certain streams. Diazotrophs may have a selective advantage in streams with low N loading. The same may be true for microniches where fixed N could be locally limiting, even in bulk sediments that do not appear to be N-limited. Channeling of fixed N compounds from cyanobacteria to attendant bacterial communities is well known (Scott and Marcarelli 2012). The coupling of diazotrophs to symbiotic bacteria (and fungi)

</page>

<page number="9">

can affect microbial community structure more broadly and may influence stream geochemical processes beyond N$_2$ fixation and assimilation (Tank and Dodds 2003; O’Brien et al. 2007).

While correlations emerged between the rates of N cycle processes in our study, few statistically significant correlations were observed between process-level measurements and the abundance of *nifH* genes, with the exception of temperature and NH$_4$-N levels. There was a strong positive correlation of temperature with both *nifH* and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance. The abundance of *nifH* genes was not significantly correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. An explanation for the weakness of the correlation between *nifH* gene abundance and N$_2$-fixation rates is that *nifH* gene copy number simply does not reflect the activity of the gene. Examination of *nifH* transcripts would provide more insight. Diazotrophs are known with more than one copy of their *nifH* genes, which could skew ratios (Ueda et al. 1995; Zehr et al. 1997). Seasonal changes, disturbances, and changing inputs may encourage a flexible stable guild. It also is possible that the N pollution in these streams has not persisted for long enough to change the abundance and distribution of microbes in the N$_2$-fixing guild. While the abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes significantly correlated with stream type, the abundance of *nifH* genes did not. Further, there were no significant correlations between the abundance of *nifH* genes and levels of chronic nitrate loading.

We recovered a number of *nifH* gene sequences from sediment clone libraries that mainly clustered with oligotrophic taxa associated with diazotrophy in soils. There were sequences from *Deltaproteobacteria* in all stream types for instance. A variety of Rhizobia were detected, but no sequences from *Azotobacter* or *Klebsiella*. While the *nifH* primers were capable of amplifying genes from *Archaea, Chlorobium, Rhodobacter* and these others, no corresponding sequences were detected. Cyanobacterial *nifH* gene sequences were recovered from sediments and would presumably be abundant in diazotrophic algal mats. Biodiversity estimates based on *nifH* sequence libraries indicated that there were similar diazotroph guilds across stream type, maintained by substantial gene flow between communities. However, there are significant differences between the diazotroph guilds among stream types when taxa are examined. There are likely to be other microbial contributors to N$_2$ fixation in stream sediments, which could be uncovered with more robust sequencing campaigns.

Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. TABLE 1. Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). Organic matter (OM) content of standing dead stems from the natural marsh averaged 66.5%, while transplanted stems averaged 70.5% OM. The OM content of leaves attached to standing dead Fig. 1. There was no difference in OM content between natural and transplanted leaves. No significant relationships were observed between ash content and standing dead stem AR rates at any sampling time in either the natural or transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p > 0.05), nor was there a significant relationship when all the data were combined. However, when all leaf data were combined, a small but statistically significant positive relationship between ash content and AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) emerged (Fig. 5, p = 0.01, r^2 = 0.2221). In October 1991, the ash content of the epiphytic film was determined separately from that of the underlying stem. The mean ash content of epiphytic films (36.6% ash) was significantly higher than that of the underlying stems (10.1% ash, t-test, p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between the ash content of epiphytic film and AR rates (nmol C2H4 g AFDW^{-1} h^{-1}, ANOVA, p > 0.05). The average number of standing dead stems in the natural marsh was 264 stems m^{-2}, while in the transplanted marsh, average standing dead stem density was 135 stems m^{-2} (Table 2). Discussion Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses. Perhaps only the exterior portion of the older, thicker film supports active N₂ fixation. This is analogous to laminated microbial mats, in which microorganisms are buried by subsequent communities, reducing their activity by limiting light and organic matter supplies (Stal and Caumette 1994). On an areal basis, rates of N₂ fixation by the epiphytic microbial community on standing dead Spartina stems in this study ranged from 1 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ to 30 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ (Table 1). Utilizing a 3:1 conversion for ethylene:N₂ reduction (Currin 1994), this results in an estimated 0.4–14 mg N m⁻² h⁻¹. These estimates are comparable to published values of N₂ fixation in salt marsh surface sediments (Jones 1974; Hanson 1977; Carpenter et al. 1978; Patriquin and Denike 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Currin et al. 1996). Our finding of higher N₂ fixation rates associated with the epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh than the natural marsh is consistent with previous results demonstrating higher rates of N₂ fixation in transplanted marsh sediments than natural marsh sediments (Currin et al. 1996). The annual N input from epiphytic N₂ fixation can be estimated utilizing the monthly AR rates in Table 1 and the following assumptions: molar ratio of C₂H₄:N₂ fixed is 3:1 (Currin 1994), midday rates represent the average AR rate for the entire daylight period, and evening rates represent the average AR rate for the entire dark period. For the months in which we have no data for nighttime fixation, we assumed that from December to May nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at half the daytime rate, and that in the period July–November nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at a rate equal to the daytime rate (Fig. 1). This last assumption incorporates observations from diel experiments in which nighttime submerged AR incubations yielded lower AR rates than nighttime aerial incuba- Fig. 3. Thus, although July–November nighttime rates sometimes exceed daytime rates in aerial incubations, that difference may not exist when high tides occur at night. Given these assumptions, the estimated annual N input by the N2-fixing epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh represents 6.3 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. In the natural marsh, the estimated annual N input is 2.5 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. These community N2 fixation rates are comparable to annual N inputs from intertidal benthic cyanobacterial mats (Capone 1983). The areal extent of the epiphytic film on standing dead stems varies considerably from stem to stem, but usually occurs on most of the lower 20 cm of the stem and on any leaves attached to that part of the stem. Assuming 20 cm of stem with 0.5 cm diameter, plus an additional 5 cm length of leaf, the average epiphyte coverage per standing dead stem is 39 cm2. Further, assuming standing dead stem densities of 150 stems m−2 in the transplanted marsh and 265 stems m−2 in the adjacent natural marsh, estimated N2 fixation by the epiphytic film on stems would be 3.8 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the transplanted marsh and 2.6 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the natural marsh. These annual estimates are 5–10 times higher than estimates of annual epiphytic N2 fixation in Louisiana and Georgia salt marshes (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981) but are almost two orders of magnitude lower than estimates from a Florida salt marsh (Green and Edmisten 1974). The latter is probably an overestimate as it exceeds that reported from any other marine or agricultural ecosystem (see Newell et al. 1992). The AR assays conducted in this study to estimate N\(_2\) fixation associated with standing dead Spartina stems lasted 2–3 h and did not display a lag period; nor did those reported by Newell et al. (1992). Seasonal shifts in the N\(_2\)-fixing community, resulting in changes in diel patterns of N\(_2\) fixation, have been reported from several benthic marine habitats (Paerl et al. 1994; Pinckney et al. 1995). The seasonal patterns in day-night N\(_2\) fixation that we observed are similar to those that occur on surface sediments on North Carolina intertidal flats (Pinckney et al. 1995). On standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems, higher midday AR rates in the spring are attributed to the N\(_2\)-fixing activity of heterocystous cyanobacteria, primarily Calothrix spp. (Curran and Paerl 1997). It appears that a spring bloom of heterocystous or coccoid cyanobacteria occurs in both marshes, as epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates are similar in early spring incubations. However, during late summer and early fall, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation in the transplanted marsh is greater than in the natural marsh. One possible explanation is that light becomes limiting in the natural marsh as the Spartina canopy develops. Stem density and biomass was greater in the natural marsh than in the transplanted marsh during this study (Table 2; S. Broome unpublished data), and stem biomass is directly related to canopy light attenuation (Morris 1989). The potential inhibitory effect of desiccation on AR rates was not accounted for in the annual estimates of N\(_2\) fixation reported here. However, the data suggest that exposure, or emergence, inhibits AR rates only during extreme low tides, and that periods of emergence during low tide periods do not necessarily correspond with decreased epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates (Figs. 2 and 3). When desiccation does cause a decrease in AR activity, the activity is restored immediately after resubmergence (Fig. 2). Other studies of intertidal microalgal communities have also demonstrated that these microorganisms are resilient following desiccation. Jones (1980) examined the effect of desiccation on photosynthetic CO\(_2\) fixation by the epiphytic community on standing dead stems in a Georgia salt marsh, and determined that even severely desiccated stems recover CO\(_2\) fixation immediately after wetting. Similarly, Jones (1974) and Pulich and Rabalais (1987) found that desiccated intertidal ben- thic cyanobacteria responded almost immediately to the addition of water by resuming N\(_2\) fixation rates comparable to submerged specimens. Apart from any inhibitory effects on epiphytic growth or activity, desiccation probably plays an important role in maintaining the species composition of the epiphytic community on standing dead stems. Calothrix, the dominant cyanobacterial genus in most sampling periods (Curran and Paerl 1997), is often restricted to the upper intertidal in marine environments (Hanson 1977; Javor and Castenholz 1981; Stal et al. 1994), and was never identified in the surface sediment of the marshes we sampled (Curran et al. 1996). In a review of aquatic N\(_2\) fixation, Howarth et al. (1988) suggested that this process was unimportant to salt marsh N budgets, because the amount of N fixed in salt marsh sediments was less than 10% of the total N input. The calculated annual contribution of new N fixed by epiphytic communities on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in this study (2–4 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)) represents an amount almost equal to the total marsh sedimentary N\(_2\) fixation calculated by Howarth et al. (1988) (2–8 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), in effect nearly doubling the estimated amount of annual marsh N\(_2\) fixation. In contrast to N fixed in the rhizosphere, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation is probably of little direct benefit to Spartina. However, its potential importance to grazers and salt marsh nutrient cycles is not trivial. The epiphytic community provides a source of new nitrogen which may be utilized by marsh consumers, or exported from the marsh as dissolved or particulate organic N. In addition, nitrogen fixed by epiphytic microorganisms may become incorporated into standing dead Spartina tissue via fungal or bacterial activity, increasing the N content of aboveground Spartina detritus. White and Howes (1994) calculated that over half of the N in standing dead Spartina tissue is derived from external sources, and suggested that N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms may contribute new N to detrital Spartina. Similarly, the \(^{15}\)N values of standing dead Spartina tissue collected from the North Carolina marshes examined in this study indicated that microbial N\(_2\) fixation supplied N which was incorporated into detrital Spartina tissue (Curran et al. 1995). Epiphytic microalgae and the associated microbial community may be an important, although often overlooked, food resource for marsh consumers. Multiple stable isotope analysis demonstrated the role of N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in the food webs of several marsh consumers (Littorina, Uca, Fundulus spp.) in North Carolina marshes (Curran et al. 1995). Other studies have described a diverse meiofaunal community associated with algal epiphytes on Spartina stems, and the utilization of stem-dwelling meiofauna by shrimp and fish (Rutledge and Fleeger 1993; Walters et al. 1996; Gregg and Fleeger in review). Results from this study and from Newell et al. (1992) demonstrate that active N_2-fixing communities develop on standing dead Spartina stems and leaves, and that these communities can differ markedly in species composition. Further research is necessary to determine how widespread these epiphytic communities are in North American Spartina marshes, and to delineate environmental controls on their development, community composition, and N_2-fixing potential. Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. TABLE 1. Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). Organic matter (OM) content of standing dead stems from the natural marsh averaged 66.5%, while transplanted stems averaged 70.5% OM. The OM content of leaves attached to standing dead Fig. 1. Dotted line connects average AR rates from midday incubations. ○ = average monthly midday AR incubation rates, ● = average monthly morning and/or evening AR incubation rates. Error bars represent the standard error of replicate samples. stems averaged 39.4%, which was significantly lower than stem OM content (t-test, p < 0.01). There was no difference in OM content between natural and transplanted leaves. No significant relationships were observed between ash content and standing dead stem AR rates at any sampling time in either the natural or transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p > 0.05), nor was there a significant relationship when all the data were combined. However, when all leaf data were combined, a small but statistically significant positive relationship between ash content and AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) emerged (Fig. 5, p = 0.01, r^2 = 0.2221). In October 1991, the ash content of the epiphytic film was determined separately from that of the underlying stem. The mean ash content of epiphytic films (36.6% ash) was significantly higher than that of the underlying stems (10.1% ash, t-test, p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between the ash content of epiphytic film and AR rates (nmol C2H4 g AFDW^{-1} h^{-1}, ANOVA, p > 0.05). The average number of standing dead stems in the natural marsh was 264 stems m^{-2}, while in the transplanted marsh, average standing dead stem density was 135 stems m^{-2} (Table 2). Discussion Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses. Although older, more decayed stems frequently ex- Fig. 2. Effect of tidal stage on average acetylene reduction (AR) rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in September. Stems were collected over two tidal cycles from a) natural and b) transplanted salt marshes in North Carolina. Solid bars represent the mean AR rate of submerged stems collected at high tide. Lined bars represent the mean AR rate of exposed stems collected at low tide. Error bars represent the standard error of five replicate samples. Absence of bars indicates AR rates below detection limits. hibited a thicker epiphytic layer (3–5 mm), these stems did not have higher N₂ fixation rates on a surface area basis. Perhaps only the exterior portion of the older, thicker film supports active N₂ fixation. This is analogous to laminated microbial mats, in which microorganisms are buried by subsequent communities, reducing their activity by limiting light and organic matter supplies (Stal and Caumette 1994). On an areal basis, rates of N₂ fixation by the epiphytic microbial community on standing dead Spartina stems in this study ranged from 1 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ to 30 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ (Table 1). Utilizing a 3:1 conversion for ethylene:N₂ reduction (Currin 1994), this results in an estimated 0.4–14 mg N m⁻² h⁻¹. These estimates are comparable to published values of N₂ fixation in salt marsh surface sediments (Jones 1974; Hanson 1977; Carpenter et al. 1978; Patriquin and Denike 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Currin et al. 1996). Our finding of higher N₂ fixation rates associated with the epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh than the natural marsh is consistent with previous results demonstrating higher rates of N₂ fixation in transplanted marsh sediments than natural marsh sediments (Currin et al. 1996). The annual N input from epiphytic N₂ fixation can be estimated utilizing the monthly AR rates in Table 1 and the following assumptions: molar ratio of C₂H₄:N₂ fixed is 3:1 (Currin 1994), midday rates represent the average AR rate for the entire daylight period, and evening rates represent the average AR rate for the entire dark period. For the months in which we have no data for nighttime fixation, we assumed that from December to May nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at half the daytime rate, and that in the period July–November nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at a rate equal to the daytime rate (Fig. 1). This last assumption incorporates observations from diel experiments in which nighttime submerged AR incubations yielded lower AR rates than nighttime aerial incuba- Fig. 3. Lined bars represent the mean AR rate of nonwetted, exposed stems. Error bars represent the standard error of 5–10 replicate samples. Fig. 4. Hatched bars represent epiphytic film dissected from stems. Lined bars represent Spartina stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed.
