Thus, although July–November nighttime rates sometimes exceed daytime rates in aerial incubations, that difference may not exist when high tides occur at night. Given these assumptions, the estimated annual N input by the N2-fixing epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh represents 6.3 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. In the natural marsh, the estimated annual N input is 2.5 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. These community N2 fixation rates are comparable to annual N inputs from intertidal benthic cyanobacterial mats (Capone 1983). The areal extent of the epiphytic film on standing dead stems varies considerably from stem to stem, but usually occurs on most of the lower 20 cm of the stem and on any leaves attached to that part of the stem. Assuming 20 cm of stem with 0.5 cm diameter, plus an additional 5 cm length of leaf, the average epiphyte coverage per standing dead stem is 39 cm2. Further, assuming standing dead stem densities of 150 stems m−2 in the transplanted marsh and 265 stems m−2 in the adjacent natural marsh, estimated N2 fixation by the epiphytic film on stems would be 3.8 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the transplanted marsh and 2.6 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the natural marsh. These annual estimates are 5–10 times higher than estimates of annual epiphytic N2 fixation in Louisiana and Georgia salt marshes (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981) but are almost two orders of magnitude lower than estimates from a Florida salt marsh (Green and Edmisten 1974). The latter is probably an overestimate as it exceeds that reported from any other marine or agricultural ecosystem (see Newell et al. 1992). However, most rhizospheric AR assays exhibit a considerable lag time before enzyme activity is measurable (several hours to days), and the above estimates have been criticized as probably being overestimates by as much as an order of magnitude (Howarth et al. 1988). The AR assays conducted in this study to estimate N\(_2\) fixation associated with standing dead Spartina stems lasted 2–3 h and did not display a lag period; nor did those reported by Newell et al. (1992). Seasonal shifts in the N\(_2\)-fixing community, resulting in changes in diel patterns of N\(_2\) fixation, have been reported from several benthic marine habitats (Paerl et al. 1994; Pinckney et al. 1995). The seasonal patterns in day-night N\(_2\) fixation that we observed are similar to those that occur on surface sediments on North Carolina intertidal flats (Pinckney et al. 1995). On standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems, higher midday AR rates in the spring are attributed to the N\(_2\)-fixing activity of heterocystous cyanobacteria, primarily Calothrix spp. (Curran and Paerl 1997). It appears that a spring bloom of heterocystous or coccoid cyanobacteria occurs in both marshes, as epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates are similar in early spring incubations. However, during late summer and early fall, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation in the transplanted marsh is greater than in the natural marsh. One possible explanation is that light becomes limiting in the natural marsh as the Spartina canopy develops. Stem density and biomass was greater in the natural marsh than in the transplanted marsh during this study (Table 2; S. Broome unpublished data), and stem biomass is directly related to canopy light attenuation (Morris 1989). The potential inhibitory effect of desiccation on AR rates was not accounted for in the annual estimates of N\(_2\) fixation reported here. However, the data suggest that exposure, or emergence, inhibits AR rates only during extreme low tides, and that periods of emergence during low tide periods do not necessarily correspond with decreased epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates (Figs. 2 and 3). When desiccation does cause a decrease in AR activity, the activity is restored immediately after resubmergence (Fig. 2). Other studies of intertidal microalgal communities have also demonstrated that these microorganisms are resilient following desiccation. Jones (1980) examined the effect of desiccation on photosynthetic CO\(_2\) fixation by the epiphytic community on standing dead stems in a Georgia salt marsh, and determined that even severely desiccated stems recover CO\(_2\) fixation immediately after wetting. Similarly, Jones (1974) and Pulich and Rabalais (1987) found that desiccated intertidal ben- thic cyanobacteria responded almost immediately to the addition of water by resuming N\(_2\) fixation rates comparable to submerged specimens. Apart from any inhibitory effects on epiphytic growth or activity, desiccation probably plays an important role in maintaining the species composition of the epiphytic community on standing dead stems. Calothrix, the dominant cyanobacterial genus in most sampling periods (Curran and Paerl 1997), is often restricted to the upper intertidal in marine environments (Hanson 1977; Javor and Castenholz 1981; Stal et al. 1994), and was never identified in the surface sediment of the marshes we sampled (Curran et al. 1996). In a review of aquatic N\(_2\) fixation, Howarth et al. (1988) suggested that this process was unimportant to salt marsh N budgets, because the amount of N fixed in salt marsh sediments was less than 10% of the total N input. The calculated annual contribution of new N fixed by epiphytic communities on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in this study (2–4 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)) represents an amount almost equal to the total marsh sedimentary N\(_2\) fixation calculated by Howarth et al. (1988) (2–8 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), in effect nearly doubling the estimated amount of annual marsh N\(_2\) fixation. In contrast to N fixed in the rhizosphere, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation is probably of little direct benefit to Spartina. However, its potential importance to grazers and salt marsh nutrient cycles is not trivial. The epiphytic community provides a source of new nitrogen which may be utilized by marsh consumers, or exported from the marsh as dissolved or particulate organic N. In addition, nitrogen fixed by epiphytic microorganisms may become incorporated into standing dead Spartina tissue via fungal or bacterial activity, increasing the N content of aboveground Spartina detritus. White and Howes (1994) calculated that over half of the N in standing dead Spartina tissue is derived from external sources, and suggested that N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms may contribute new N to detrital Spartina. Similarly, the \(^{15}\)N values of standing dead Spartina tissue collected from the North Carolina marshes examined in this study indicated that microbial N\(_2\) fixation supplied N which was incorporated into detrital Spartina tissue (Curran et al. 1995). Epiphytic microalgae and the associated microbial community may be an important, although often overlooked, food resource for marsh consumers. Multiple stable isotope analysis demonstrated the role of N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in the food webs of several marsh consumers (Littorina, Uca, Fundulus spp.) in North Carolina marshes (Curran et al. 1995). Other studies have described a diverse meiofaunal community associated with algal epiphytes on Spartina stems, and the utilization of stem-dwelling meiofauna by shrimp and fish (Rutledge and Fleeger 1993; Walters et al. 1996; Gregg and Fleeger in review). Results from this study and from Newell et al. (1992) demonstrate that active N_2-fixing communities develop on standing dead Spartina stems and leaves, and that these communities can differ markedly in species composition. Further research is necessary to determine how widespread these epiphytic communities are in North American Spartina marshes, and to delineate environmental controls on their development, community composition, and N_2-fixing potential. Effects of Lake Size on Nutrient Availability in the Mixed Layer during Summer Stratification E.J. Fee, R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Central and Arctic Region, Freshwater Institute, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6, Canada Fee, E.J., R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson. 1994. Effects of lake size on nutrient availability in the mixed layer during summer stratification. Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 51: 2756–2768. Fluxes to the summer mixed layer of N, Si, and P were estimated in a size series of northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Increasing turbulence caused upward fluxes through the thermocline to increase with lake size for nutrients that increased in concentration below the thermocline (soluble reactive Si, total inorganic N, and NO_3^−; but not total N or any form of P). Precipitation and terrestrial runoff were equally important sources of N and P in all but very small lakes (<100 ha), where precipitation supplied much more than runoff. Runoff was the only important source of Si, except in very large lakes (> 100 000 ha) where mixing through the thermocline was important. N_2-fixation was unimportant except in intermediate-sized lakes (700–2000 ha). Si fluxes nearly equaled phytoplankton requirements, but N and P were below requirements, and recycling within the mixed layer must be the most important source of these nutrients. N and P deficits increased progressively with lake size, implying that the efficiency of nutrient recycling increased with lake size; mixed layers in large lakes are more turbulent and thicker than in small lakes and these processes increase the probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer. Les flux de N, de Si et de P vers la couche de mélange estivale ont été estimés dans des lacs de différentes tailles du Bouclier canadien dans le nord-ouest de l’Ontario. Une turbulence accrue donne lieu à une augmentation proportionnelle à la taille des lacs des flux ascendants dans la thermocline dans le cas des éléments nutritifs dont la concentration augmente sous la thermocline (Si réactif soluble, N inorganique total, et NO_3^−); mais non le N total et aucune forme de P). Les précipitations et le ruissellement de surface étaient des sources de N et de P d’égale importance dans tous les lacs, sauf dans les très petits (<100 ha), où la contribution des précipitations étaient beaucoup plus importante à cet égard. Le ruissellement était la seule source importante de Si, sauf sans les très grands lacs (> 100 000 ha), où le mélange dans la thermocline apportait une contribution importante. La fixation du N_2 n’était pas importante sauf dans les lacs de taille intermédiaire (700–2 000 ha). Les flux de Si satisfaisaient presque les besoins du phytoplancton alors que ceux de N et de P étaient insuffisants, le recyclage dans la couche de mélange assurant probablement le principal apport de ces deux derniers éléments. Les carences en N et en P allaient en s’accroissant avec la taille des lacs, ce qui implique que la contribution du recyclage des éléments nutritifs s’accroît avec la taille des lacs; en effet, les couches de mélange des grands lacs sont plus turbulentes et plus épaisses que celles des petits lacs, ce qui accroît les possibilités de régénération des éléments nutritifs dans la couche de mélange. Received September 21, 1993 Accepted July 12, 1994 (J12098) Reçu le 21 septembre 1993 Accepté le 12 juillet 1994 When Johnson and Vallentyne (1971) introduced the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) program in the scientific literature, they clearly recognized that extrapolation of results obtained from the observation and manipulation of very small lakes to larger, more economically important ones was a fundamental assumption of ELA’s design. They presented several examples of how a lake’s size might affect critical limnological processes and stated that these “... must be taken into account in any extrapolation.” Yet for nearly two decades, ELA results have been extrapolated to larger lakes without any explicit consideration of such effects. The Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) program (Fee and Hecky 1992) was designed to remedy this deficiency; specifically, the purpose of NOLSS is to investigate physical gradients associated with lake size and to determine their biological significance. In an initial NOLSS publication, Fee et al. (1992) reported that annual rates of phytoplankton photosynthesis (PP) per unit of lake surface area (i.e., areal PP) increased progressively with lake size simply because larger lakes were ice free for longer periods and had thicker mixed layers than small lakes. In contrast, these authors showed that annual rates of PP per unit volume of the mixed layer (volumetric PP) varied with lake size in a bell-shaped pattern, i.e., rates in the smallest and largest lakes (29 ha ELA Lake 373 and 8 × 10^6 ha Lake Superior, respectively) were low and similar, whereas midsized lakes had rates nearly an order of magnitude greater. Fee et al. (1992) hypothesized that this pattern resulted from systematic changes of turbulence and water temperature with increasing lake size. According to this hypothesis, the increasing intensity of turbulence with 1This is one in a series of papers describing work of the Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory on a lake-size series in Northwest Ontario. It is also a contribution to the series honoring the 25th anniversary of the Experimental Lakes Area. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Results The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the hypolimnia of small lakes (top three panels in the left columns of Fig. 2 and 3); gradients were much smaller in larger lakes (right column of panels in Fig. 2 and 3). However, mixing fluxes through the thermocline depend only on concentration gradients at the depth of the thermocline (Equation (1)), and there was no obvious relationship between gradients at this depth and lake size (Table 2). Thus, lake-to-lake differences in the upward flux of individual nutrients through the thermocline depend almost entirely on \( K_z \), which was more than two orders of magnitude greater in the largest lake (Nipigon) than in the smallest (ELA Lake 373) (Table 2). Fluxes increased progressively with lake size for those nutrients that increased in concentration with depth in the region of the thermocline (NO₃⁻, TIN, and SRSi) but were nil for nutrients that had zero or negative gradients (TN, TDP, TP). Over a 21-yr period, the summer mixed layer of ELA Lake 239 received similar amounts of TN and TP from precipitation and terrestrial runoff (Fig. 4). There was always much more TIN and NO₃⁻ in precipitation than in runoff, but runoff was by far the most important source of Si. In 1990, upward mixing through the thermocline was an important source of nutrients (compared with precipitation and runoff) only in lakes >1000 ha (Table 3). The amount of N supplied by N₂-fixation was much less than that supplied by precipitation and runoff except in intermediate-sized lakes; why higher N₂-fixation rates occurred in these lakes is unclear, because other fluxes of N to them were not unusually low. Interannually, fluxes from precipitation and terrestrial runoff varied by about the same amount as did nutrient concentration gradients in the thermocline of Lake 239 (Fig. 5); the coefficients of variation of NO₃⁻ in precipitation and of concentration gradients of NO₃⁻ in the Lake 239 thermocline were both 40%. Figure 5 also shows that in 1990 (the only year for which we have the chemistry depth profile data required to estimate vertical mixing fluxes in the NOLSS lakes) vertical concentration gradients in Lake 239 were unusually low. If interannual variations of chemical concentration gradients in Lake 239 also occur in larger lakes, then mixing fluxes would be about double those given in Table 2 in an average year, and up to three times greater in high years. In 1990, fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer fell far short of phytoplankton requirements (Table 3 and left column of panels in Fig. 6), but the deficit of Si was slight. Discussion Turbulent mixing through the thermocline, the only nutrient flux to the mixed layer that is explicitly dependent on lake size, supplied less TN and TP than did those fluxes that are independent of lake size (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, N\(_2\)-fixation; Fig. 6). Mixing supplied more of some forms of N (NO\(_3^-\) and TIN) and of SRSi in larger than in smaller lakes (Table 3), but terrestrial runoff more than made up for the SRSi that turbulence failed to supply in small lakes. Thus, the only mixing fluxes of potential ecological importance are of NO\(_3^-\) and TIN. Although N plays an important role in determining phytoplankton community composition (Schindler 1977), it rarely limits algal biomass in unperturbed Canadian Shield lakes (Hecky and Kilham 1988). We, therefore, conclude that the turbulence-mediated upward flux of nutrients through the summer thermocline was an insignificant component of mixed-layer nutrient budgets in all sizes of Canadian Shield lakes in 1990. We did not measure concentrations of PO\(_4^{3-}\), the form of P most readily assimilated by phytoplankton, because standard chemical methods for measuring it always overestimate actual concentrations in Canadian Shield lakes (Stainton 1980). Moreover, when special radiochemical methods have been used to measure it, concentrations in these lakes were always minute (<0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler 1980). Nevertheless, if PO\(_4^{3-}\) did increase in concentration with depth in the thermoclines of the lakes we studied, we may have missed an important source of this critical element. We obtained an upper bound on the magnitude of this flux by assuming that concentrations increase from 0 in the mixed layer to the highest summer values ever measured in the hypolimnia of unperturbed northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes (0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler, 1980) over a distance of 1 m in all the lakes. These extremely generous assumptions yield upward (mixing) fluxes of P on the order of 0.002 \( \mu \)mol·m\(^{-2}\)·d\(^{-1} \), which amounts to only ~0.001% of the amount of P that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer require. We thus confidently conclude that the upward flux of PO\(_4^{3-}\) through the thermocline is insignificant in Canadian Shield lakes. None of the foregoing conclusions depend critically on our use of Equation (2) to estimate \( K_z \), which is a statistical fit to the results of Mortimer (1941), Jassby and Powell (1975), Hutchinson (1957), Hesslein and Quay (1973), and Ward (1977). Two of these papers (Mortimer’s and Hutchinson’s), in turn, summarize results from many other independent studies. A possible objection to these results, however, is that with one exception they are all based on measurements of the rate at which heat moved downward through the thermocline. The exception was Hesslein and Quay (1973), who found that in a very small, deep lake (ELA Lake 227; \( A_0 = 5 \) ha, \( z_m = 10 \) m) \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of a dissolved material (radon gas) was much smaller than \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of heat. This happened because turbulence was so low that transport was almost entirely the result of molecular diffusion, and heat has a higher coefficient of molecular conductivity than radon gas. Because all of our lakes are much larger than Lake 227, they have \( K_z \) values substantially greater than the molecular conductivity of heat, and this cannot be a problem here. Moreover, if \( K_z \) were smaller than the values we derived from Equation (2), vertical fluxes would be even smaller than those we calculated, which we have already concluded to be insignificant. Finally, because concentration gradients of all forms of P in the region of the thermocline were negligible, our conclusion that vertical fluxes of this critical element were nil in all lake sizes is completely independent of \( K_z \). Figure 6 shows that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer required much more P and N than all of the fluxes measured in 1990. The deficit of supply relative to demand was notably greater for P than for N, further confirming that P is the most limiting nutrient in Canadian Shield lakes (Schindler 1977, 1988; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1988; Levine and Schindler 1992; Hecky et al. 1993; S. Another possible problem with our approach is that we assume that Fee et al.’s (1992) \(^{14}\)C-based PP values estimate daily net C fixation into particles. We emphasize that our use of the term “net” is distinct from another common use of this term, i.e., the amount of material exported from the primary trophic level during an entire growing season (stored in sediments, flushed out of the lake, or converted into the flesh of higher trophic levels). We make no assumption about what happens to particles over periods longer than a day. Bower et al. (1987) showed that in an ELA whole-lake \(^{14}\)C experiment, Fee et al.’s (1992) PP method closely approximated net daily incorporation of C into particles; all losses of \(^{14}\)C from particles occurred at night, and these losses averaged only 8% of the daytime rate of incorporation of inorganic C into particulate matter (range 3–17%, \(n = 13\)). Essentially, we explicitly ignore this small and variable correction, and assume that the \(^{14}\)C method used by Fee et al. (1992) yields estimates of daily net particulate C fixation; Peterson (1978) reported that this is true for rapidly growing algal cultures. The final critical basic assumption for our analysis is that all major nutrient fluxes to the mixed layer were measured. One potential nutrient source that we did not measure is that from epilimnion sediments. However, studies at ELA have repeatedly demonstrated that epilimnion sediments return little or no P to the water column (\(^{32}\)P measurements: Schindler et al. 1975; Levine et al. 1986; mass balance calculations: Schindler et al. 1973, 1987; Levine and Schindler 1989; porewater gradient measurements: Schindler et al. 1977; L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Levine and Schindler (1989) did find that littoral sediments supplied N to the mixed layer, but as mentioned above, N rarely limits phytoplankton biomass in Canadian Shield lakes. Moreover, Levine and Schindler (1992) showed that the N returned to the water column from epilimnetic sediments was almost entirely derived from materials recently deposited at the sediment–water interface, rather than from deep within the sediment itself; in our view, this constitutes nutrient recycling within the mixed layer. We thus conclude that Fig. 6 can be accepted at face value, and that fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer were a small fraction of the physiological requirements of phytoplankton in 1990. Indeed, these fluxes would be capable of meeting phytoplankton needs only in small lakes and if the most generous assumptions about supply and demand are made. The major implication is that recycling within the mixed layer must be the major source of N and P for algae living there. This is scarcely a new or surprising conclusion. Harrison (1980, and see references therein) showed that external inputs of N, P, and Si to the sea could account for <1% of the amounts required by phytoplankton, and he concluded that recycling supplied the remainder. In fresh water, Levine and Schindler (1980) found that in an unfertilized, stratified ELA lake (Lake 302S; \(A_0 = 10.9\) ha, \(z_m = 10.6\) m) an average P atom recycled through epilimnetic seston 17 times prior to being lost from the mixed layer, and Levine et al. (1986, p. 376) stated that “... the predominant source of phosphate for phytoplankton in the epilimnion is not external supply, but recycling.” This result has been corroborated by so many independent studies (see Planas and Hecky 1984, and references therein) that it would have been extremely surprising if our results contradicted it. Figure 6 illustrates what may be our single most important result, viz., the fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements accounted for by all estimated fluxes to the mixed layer systematically decreases with increasing lake size. That is, nutrient recycling within the mixed layer supplies a progressively increasing fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements as lake size increases. This is logical, because both the intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the thickness of the mixed layer increase with lake size. As a consequence, mixed-layer particle residence times increase with lake size; this increases the probability that particle-bound nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than being lost to the sediments. A lower bound on the magnitude of this effect can be derived using Hesslein et al.’s (1980) value of 0.18 m·d\(^{-1}\) for the settling rate of particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 224 (\(A_0 = 25.9\) ha, \(z_m = 27\) m). Applying this figure to all lake sizes, it would take 33 d for settling to remove all particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 373 (\(z_{th} = 6\) m) compared with 72 d in Trout Lake (\(z_{th} = 13\) m). However, because large lakes have much more turbulent mixed layers than small ones, the actual difference in particle residence times in large versus small lakes is undoubtedly even greater. The percent organic C in deep-water sediments declines in a strikingly regular fashion with increasing lake size (Fig. 7). This result strongly supports our conclusion that the rate of nutrient recycling within the mixed layer increases with increasing lake size. The longer that particles are retained in the mixed layer, the more likely it is that the C they contain will be respired back to CO\(_2\) and lost to the atmosphere rather than falling through the thermocline and accumulating in deep-water sediments. We do not believe that recycling is the only process responsible for producing this pattern. Indeed, such regularity is probably the product of many processes acting in concert (e.g., longer retention in the mixed layer, increasing total depth of the water column, decreasing terrestrial influence, etc.). Nevertheless, it is fully consonant with our conclusion that large lakes recycle nutrients more efficiently than small ones. The greater efficiency of nutrient recycling in the mixed layer in large than in small lakes has important implications for Fee's (1979) theory that the rate of nutrient recycling is a function of basin morphometry. He found that in small ELA lakes, the area of epilimnion sediments (\(A_e\)) divided by the volume of the epilimnion (\(V_e\)) was strongly correlated with rates of volumetric PP. He demonstrated that, if all other factors are equal, \(A_e/V_e\) is mathematically equivalent to the probability of retention of particles in the mixed layer and thus parameterized the rate of nutrient recycling. He cautioned that this might not be true in larger lakes, where processes that are negligible in small lakes could affect nutrient recycling. Our results bear out this prediction; as lakes increase in size, the increasing intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the increasing thickness of the mixed layer both retard sedimentation losses through the thermocline, thereby increasing mixed layer particle residence time. Consequently, a large lake with a low \(A_e/V_e\) value and a small lake with a high \(A_e/V_e\) value could have the same mixed layer particle residence times and similar rates of nutrient recycling. An important corollary is that large and small lakes with similar \(A_e/V_e\) values should respond differently to the same external P loading. Productivity should be higher in the large lake because of its higher rate of nutrient recycling. These results lend strong support to Margalef's (1974) theory that physical energy levels directly control food-web structures and the biogeochemical characteristics of water bodies. The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the water column of small lakes (Fig. 2 and 3); in contrast, large lakes had relatively well-mixed hypolimnia with maximum gradients at or just below the thermocline. This difference is probably the result of several processes: (1) Internal waves, which are the primary source of hypolimnetic turbulence, are significant only in lakes with surface areas >1000 ha (Boyce 1974); thus, in small lakes, nutrients from particles remineralized near the bottom of the water column move upward very slowly compared with larger lakes. (2) Sediment focussing is very important in small lakes (Anderson et al. 1987) and causes particles that fall through the thermocline to move rapidly to great depths. (3) Because small lakes have shallow mixed layers, significant quantities of light penetrate below their thermoclines (Fee et al. 1991), permitting large algal populations to develop deep in their water columns (Fee 1976). These algal populations intercept nutrients diffusing up from below and prevent them from reaching the thermocline. Schindler and Nighswander (1970) and Bayley et al. (1992) reported that precipitation was the major source of N and P to Canadian Shield lakes. However, their conclusion was based on results obtained from the study of quite small lakes. Our results (Fig. 6) indicate that this does not apply to Canadian Shield lakes >300 ha, where fluxes of N and P from terrestrial runoff and precipitation were very similar in magnitude. Unlike N and P, there was virtually no Si in precipitation, and mixing supplied substantial quantities of this nutrient only in very large lakes (Fig. 6). However, terrestrial runoff of Si was large, particularly in small and midsized lakes, and the sum of all the fluxes that we measured apparently match phytoplankton requirements. There must, therefore, be some reason, other than a lack of supply, for why diatoms are unimportant components of the summer phytoplankton community in small, stratified Canadian Shield lakes (Kling and Holmgren 1972; Findlay and Kasian 1990). Again, the most likely explanation is based on the low mixed-layer turbulence and shallow mixed-layer depths in small lakes. Theoretically, the higher specific gravity of diatoms gives them a selective advantage over nonsinking or weakly motile competitors because by sinking they increase the rate at which they contact dissolved nutrients (by thinning the nutrient-depleted boundary layer that surrounds them: Hutchinson 1967; Margalef 1974; Titman and Kilham 1976). This strategy works well in large lakes, where high turbulence and deep mixed layers keep cells from being rapidly lost by sedimentation through the thermocline. Diatoms are also well represented in small, unstratified lakes, which lack a hypolimnion sedimentation trap altogether (Kling and Holmgren 1972). However, this strategy apparently fails in small, stratified lakes where shallow mixed layers and relatively stable water columns lead to rapid removal of sinking cells from the mixed layer. Conclusion The increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size acted in concert with positive concentration gradients of NO\(_3^-\), TDN, and SRSi in the region of the thermocline to result in more of these nutrients being transported upwards through the thermoclines in large than in small lakes (Table 2). These nutrients, however, rarely limit phytoplankton growth in Canadian Shield lakes. Because concentration gradients of P, the nutrient that does limit algal growth in Canadian Shield lakes, were nil in the region of the thermocline in all of these lakes (Fig. 2 and 3; Table 2), upward fluxes of P were essentially zero in all lake sizes. Our results support Fee et al.'s (1992) hypothesis that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP. It does this by acting in concert with the increasing depth of the mixed layer to cause particles to be retained in the mixed layer longer, thus increasing the probability that nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than lost to the sediments. Our results do not, however, rule out the possibility that the greater rates of volumetric PP in midsized lakes reported by Fee et al. (1992) are caused by lake-to-lake differences of external P loading. That is, although our results show that, all other things being equal, higher turbulence and thicker mixed layers enhance nutrient recycling and lead to higher rates of areal PP in larger lakes, the approach we have taken of using runoff and precipitation data measured in the basin of one small ELA lake to estimate P loading in all the other lakes has inherent inaccuracies (Fee and Hecky 1992). External P loading within this lake-size series could vary enough to explain the observed differences of volumetric PP. Nevertheless, Fee et al. (1992) showed that it is unlikely that areal PP, which theoretically sets potential yields of higher trophic levels, is the result of lake-to-lake differences in external P loading. Our main conclusion, that the probability of regeneration of nutrients within the mixed layer increases with lake size, has an important corollary: external nutrient loads should be converted into higher trophic levels, including especially valued organisms such as fish, more efficiently in large than in small lakes. This prediction is in harmony with Nixon's (1988) conclusion that the greatest standing crops of benthos and highest fish yields come from the most energetic marine environments. He further noted that, as we found in large lakes, sediments from these highly productive regions contained less C than did sediments from less energetic environments. His interpretation of these observations was also the same as ours, viz., that energetic mixed layers recycle nutrients more efficiently than less energetic ones. Effects of Lake Size on Nutrient Availability in the Mixed Layer during Summer Stratification E.J. Fee, R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Central and Arctic Region, Freshwater Institute, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6, Canada Fee, E.J., R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson. 1994. Effects of lake size on nutrient availability in the mixed layer during summer stratification. Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 51: 2756–2768. Fluxes to the summer mixed layer of N, Si, and P were estimated in a size series of northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Increasing turbulence caused upward fluxes through the thermocline to increase with lake size for nutrients that increased in concentration below the thermocline (soluble reactive Si, total inorganic N, and NO_3^−; but not total N or any form of P). Precipitation and terrestrial runoff were equally important sources of N and P in all but very small lakes (<100 ha), where precipitation supplied much more than runoff. Runoff was the only important source of Si, except in very large lakes (> 100 000 ha) where mixing through the thermocline was important. N_2-fixation was unimportant except in intermediate-sized lakes (700–2000 ha). Si fluxes nearly equaled phytoplankton requirements, but N and P were below requirements, and recycling within the mixed layer must be the most important source of these nutrients. N and P deficits increased progressively with lake size, implying that the efficiency of nutrient recycling increased with lake size; mixed layers in large lakes are more turbulent and thicker than in small lakes and these processes increase the probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer. Les flux de N, de Si et de P vers la couche de mélange estivale ont été estimés dans des lacs de différentes tailles du Bouclier canadien dans le nord-ouest de l’Ontario. Une turbulence accrue donne lieu à une augmentation proportionnelle à la taille des lacs des flux ascendants dans la thermocline dans le cas des éléments nutritifs dont la concentration augmente sous la thermocline (Si réactif soluble, N inorganique total, et NO_3^−); mais non le N total et aucune forme de P). Les précipitations et le ruissellement de surface étaient des sources de N et de P d’égale importance dans tous les lacs, sauf dans les très petits (<100 ha), où la contribution des précipitations étaient beaucoup plus importante à cet égard. Le ruissellement était la seule source importante de Si, sauf sans les très grands lacs (> 100 000 ha), où le mélange dans la thermocline apportait une contribution importante. La fixation du N_2 n’était pas importante sauf dans les lacs de taille intermédiaire (700–2 000 ha). Les flux de Si satisfaisaient presque les besoins du phytoplancton alors que ceux de N et de P étaient insuffisants, le recyclage dans la couche de mélange assurant probablement le principal apport de ces deux derniers éléments. Les carences en N et en P allaient en s’accroissant avec la taille des lacs, ce qui implique que la contribution du recyclage des éléments nutritifs s’accroît avec la taille des lacs; en effet, les couches de mélange des grands lacs sont plus turbulentes et plus épaisses que celles des petits lacs, ce qui accroît les possibilités de régénération des éléments nutritifs dans la couche de mélange. Received September 21, 1993 Accepted July 12, 1994 (J12098) Reçu le 21 septembre 1993 Accepté le 12 juillet 1994 When Johnson and Vallentyne (1971) introduced the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) program in the scientific literature, they clearly recognized that extrapolation of results obtained from the observation and manipulation of very small lakes to larger, more economically important ones was a fundamental assumption of ELA’s design. They presented several examples of how a lake’s size might affect critical limnological processes and stated that these “... must be taken into account in any extrapolation.” Yet for nearly two decades, ELA results have been extrapolated to larger lakes without any explicit consideration of such effects. The Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) program (Fee and Hecky 1992) was designed to remedy this deficiency; specifically, the purpose of NOLSS is to investigate physical gradients associated with lake size and to determine their biological significance. In an initial NOLSS publication, Fee et al. (1992) reported that annual rates of phytoplankton photosynthesis (PP) per unit of lake surface area (i.e., areal PP) increased progressively with lake size simply because larger lakes were ice free for longer periods and had thicker mixed layers than small lakes. In contrast, these authors showed that annual rates of PP per unit volume of the mixed layer (volumetric PP) varied with lake size in a bell-shaped pattern, i.e., rates in the smallest and largest lakes (29 ha ELA Lake 373 and 8 × 10^6 ha Lake Superior, respectively) were low and similar, whereas midsized lakes had rates nearly an order of magnitude greater. Fee et al. (1992) hypothesized that this pattern resulted from systematic changes of turbulence and water temperature with increasing lake size. According to this hypothesis, the increasing intensity of turbulence with 1This is one in a series of papers describing work of the Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory on a lake-size series in Northwest Ontario. It is also a contribution to the series honoring the 25th anniversary of the Experimental Lakes Area. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Water chemistry depth profiles were determined twice: once at the beginning and again at the end of summer stratification (mid-June and late August, except in Trout Lake and Lake Nipigon, where corresponding temperature stratification conditions occurred in early July and mid-September); chemistry profiles were not measured on Orange Lake or Lake Superior. A PVC Van Dorn bottle was used to collect water samples, which were transported to the laboratory in polyethylene bottles precleaned with dilute HCl, followed by three rinses of distilled water, and then air-dried. Total inorganic N (TIN = \( NO_3^- + NO_2^- + NH_4^+ \)), total P (TP = TDP + SPP), and total N (TN = TDN + SPN) were obtained arithmetically. Orthophosphate (\( PO_4^{3-} \)) is undetectable in these waters (Stainton 1980). Turbulence-mediated nutrient fluxes up through the thermocline (mass\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\)) were multiplied by the ratio of the area of the lake at the depth of the thermocline (\( A_{th} \)) to the surface area of the lake (\( A_0 \)) (Table 2); this renders them directly comparable with other fluxes to the mixed layer (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation) and to the nutrient requirements of phytoplankton, which were based on the rate of phytoplankton photosynthesis per square metre of lake surface, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth (Fee 1980). Chemical concentrations were not measured in Orange Lake or Lake Superior; mixing fluxes thus cannot be calculated for these lakes directly. Mixing fluxes in Orange Lake were estimated by interpolating linearly (lake surface area being the independent variable) from those measured in Green and Linge Lakes. Because Lake Superior is the largest member of the size series, this method cannot be used and mixing fluxes are not available for this lake. Results The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the hypolimnia of small lakes (top three panels in the left columns of Fig. 2 and 3); gradients were much smaller in larger lakes (right column of panels in Fig. 2 and 3). However, mixing fluxes through the thermocline depend only on concentration gradients at the depth of the thermocline (Equation (1)), and there was no obvious relationship between gradients at this depth and lake size (Table 2). Thus, lake-to-lake differences in the upward flux of individual nutrients through the thermocline depend almost entirely on \( K_z \), which was more than two orders of magnitude greater in the largest lake (Nipigon) than in the smallest (ELA Lake 373) (Table 2). Fluxes increased progressively with lake size for those nutrients that increased in concentration with depth in the region of the thermocline (NO₃⁻, TIN, and SRSi) but were nil for nutrients that had zero or negative gradients (TN, TDP, TP). Over a 21-yr period, the summer mixed layer of ELA Lake 239 received similar amounts of TN and TP from precipitation and terrestrial runoff (Fig. 4). There was always much more TIN and NO₃⁻ in precipitation than in runoff, but runoff was by far the most important source of Si. In 1990, upward mixing through the thermocline was an important source of nutrients (compared with precipitation and runoff) only in lakes >1000 ha (Table 3). The amount of N supplied by N₂-fixation was much less than that supplied by precipitation and runoff except in intermediate-sized lakes; why higher N₂-fixation rates occurred in these lakes is unclear, because other fluxes of N to them were not unusually low. Interannually, fluxes from precipitation and terrestrial runoff varied by about the same amount as did nutrient concentration gradients in the thermocline of Lake 239 (Fig. 5); the coefficients of variation of NO₃⁻ in precipitation and of concentration gradients of NO₃⁻ in the Lake 239 thermocline were both 40%. Figure 5 also shows that in 1990 (the only year for which we have the chemistry depth profile data required to estimate vertical mixing fluxes in the NOLSS lakes) vertical concentration gradients in Lake 239 were unusually low. If interannual variations of chemical concentration gradients in Lake 239 also occur in larger lakes, then mixing fluxes would be about double those given in Table 2 in an average year, and up to three times greater in high years. In 1990, fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer fell far short of phytoplankton requirements (Table 3 and left column of panels in Fig. 6), but the deficit of Si was slight. Discussion Turbulent mixing through the thermocline, the only nutrient flux to the mixed layer that is explicitly dependent on lake size, supplied less TN and TP than did those fluxes that are independent of lake size (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, N\(_2\)-fixation; Fig. 6). Mixing supplied more of some forms of N (NO\(_3^-\) and TIN) and of SRSi in larger than in smaller lakes (Table 3), but terrestrial runoff more than made up for the SRSi that turbulence failed to supply in small lakes. Thus, the only mixing fluxes of potential ecological importance are of NO\(_3^-\) and TIN. Although N plays an important role in determining phytoplankton community composition (Schindler 1977), it rarely limits algal biomass in unperturbed Canadian Shield lakes (Hecky and Kilham 1988). We, therefore, conclude that the turbulence-mediated upward flux of nutrients through the summer thermocline was an insignificant component of mixed-layer nutrient budgets in all sizes of Canadian Shield lakes in 1990. We did not measure concentrations of PO\(_4^{3-}\), the form of P most readily assimilated by phytoplankton, because standard chemical methods for measuring it always overestimate actual concentrations in Canadian Shield lakes (Stainton 1980). Moreover, when special radiochemical methods have been used to measure it, concentrations in these lakes were always minute (<0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler 1980). Nevertheless, if PO\(_4^{3-}\) did increase in concentration with depth in the thermoclines of the lakes we studied, we may have missed an important source of this critical element. We obtained an upper bound on the magnitude of this flux by assuming that concentrations increase from 0 in the mixed layer to the highest summer values ever measured in the hypolimnia of unperturbed northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes (0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler, 1980) over a distance of 1 m in all the lakes. These extremely generous assumptions yield upward (mixing) fluxes of P on the order of 0.002 \( \mu \)mol·m\(^{-2}\)·d\(^{-1} \), which amounts to only ~0.001% of the amount of P that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer require. We thus confidently conclude that the upward flux of PO\(_4^{3-}\) through the thermocline is insignificant in Canadian Shield lakes. None of the foregoing conclusions depend critically on our use of Equation (2) to estimate \( K_z \), which is a statistical fit to the results of Mortimer (1941), Jassby and Powell (1975), Hutchinson (1957), Hesslein and Quay (1973), and Ward (1977). Two of these papers (Mortimer’s and Hutchinson’s), in turn, summarize results from many other independent studies. A possible objection to these results, however, is that with one exception they are all based on measurements of the rate at which heat moved downward through the thermocline. The exception was Hesslein and Quay (1973), who found that in a very small, deep lake (ELA Lake 227; \( A_0 = 5 \) ha, \( z_m = 10 \) m) \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of a dissolved material (radon gas) was much smaller than \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of heat. This happened because turbulence was so low that transport was almost entirely the result of molecular diffusion, and heat has a higher coefficient of molecular conductivity than radon gas. Because all of our lakes are much larger than Lake 227, they have \( K_z \) values substantially greater than the molecular conductivity of heat, and this cannot be a problem here. Moreover, if \( K_z \) were smaller than the values we derived from Equation (2), vertical fluxes would be even smaller than those we calculated, which we have already concluded to be insignificant. Finally, because concentration gradients of all forms of P in the region of the thermocline were negligible, our conclusion that vertical fluxes of this critical element were nil in all lake sizes is completely independent of \( K_z \). Figure 6 shows that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer required much more P and N than all of the fluxes measured in 1990. The deficit of supply relative to demand was notably greater for P than for N, further confirming that P is the most limiting nutrient in Canadian Shield lakes (Schindler 1977, 1988; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1988; Levine and Schindler 1992; Hecky et al. 1993; S. Another possible problem with our approach is that we assume that Fee et al.’s (1992) \(^{14}\)C-based PP values estimate daily net C fixation into particles. We emphasize that our use of the term “net” is distinct from another common use of this term, i.e., the amount of material exported from the primary trophic level during an entire growing season (stored in sediments, flushed out of the lake, or converted into the flesh of higher trophic levels). We make no assumption about what happens to particles over periods longer than a day. Bower et al. (1987) showed that in an ELA whole-lake \(^{14}\)C experiment, Fee et al.’s (1992) PP method closely approximated net daily incorporation of C into particles; all losses of \(^{14}\)C from particles occurred at night, and these losses averaged only 8% of the daytime rate of incorporation of inorganic C into particulate matter (range 3–17%, \(n = 13\)). Essentially, we explicitly ignore this small and variable correction, and assume that the \(^{14}\)C method used by Fee et al. (1992) yields estimates of daily net particulate C fixation; Peterson (1978) reported that this is true for rapidly growing algal cultures. The final critical basic assumption for our analysis is that all major nutrient fluxes to the mixed layer were measured. One potential nutrient source that we did not measure is that from epilimnion sediments. However, studies at ELA have repeatedly demonstrated that epilimnion sediments return little or no P to the water column (\(^{32}\)P measurements: Schindler et al. 1975; Levine et al. 1986; mass balance calculations: Schindler et al. 1973, 1987; Levine and Schindler 1989; porewater gradient measurements: Schindler et al. 1977; L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Levine and Schindler (1989) did find that littoral sediments supplied N to the mixed layer, but as mentioned above, N rarely limits phytoplankton biomass in Canadian Shield lakes. Moreover, Levine and Schindler (1992) showed that the N returned to the water column from epilimnetic sediments was almost entirely derived from materials recently deposited at the sediment–water interface, rather than from deep within the sediment itself; in our view, this constitutes nutrient recycling within the mixed layer. We thus conclude that Fig. 6 can be accepted at face value, and that fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer were a small fraction of the physiological requirements of phytoplankton in 1990. Indeed, these fluxes would be capable of meeting phytoplankton needs only in small lakes and if the most generous assumptions about supply and demand are made. The major implication is that recycling within the mixed layer must be the major source of N and P for algae living there. This is scarcely a new or surprising conclusion. Harrison (1980, and see references therein) showed that external inputs of N, P, and Si to the sea could account for <1% of the amounts required by phytoplankton, and he concluded that recycling supplied the remainder. In fresh water, Levine and Schindler (1980) found that in an unfertilized, stratified ELA lake (Lake 302S; \(A_0 = 10.9\) ha, \(z_m = 10.6\) m) an average P atom recycled through epilimnetic seston 17 times prior to being lost from the mixed layer, and Levine et al. (1986, p. 376) stated that “... the predominant source of phosphate for phytoplankton in the epilimnion is not external supply, but recycling.” This result has been corroborated by so many independent studies (see Planas and Hecky 1984, and references therein) that it would have been extremely surprising if our results contradicted it. Figure 6 illustrates what may be our single most important result, viz., the fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements accounted for by all estimated fluxes to the mixed layer systematically decreases with increasing lake size. That is, nutrient recycling within the mixed layer supplies a progressively increasing fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements as lake size increases. This is logical, because both the intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the thickness of the mixed layer increase with lake size. As a consequence, mixed-layer particle residence times increase with lake size; this increases the probability that particle-bound nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than being lost to the sediments. A lower bound on the magnitude of this effect can be derived using Hesslein et al.’s (1980) value of 0.18 m·d\(^{-1}\) for the settling rate of particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 224 (\(A_0 = 25.9\) ha, \(z_m = 27\) m). Applying this figure to all lake sizes, it would take 33 d for settling to remove all particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 373 (\(z_{th} = 6\) m) compared with 72 d in Trout Lake (\(z_{th} = 13\) m). However, because large lakes have much more turbulent mixed layers than small ones, the actual difference in particle residence times in large versus small lakes is undoubtedly even greater. The percent organic C in deep-water sediments declines in a strikingly regular fashion with increasing lake size (Fig. 7). This result strongly supports our conclusion that the rate of nutrient recycling within the mixed layer increases with increasing lake size. The longer that particles are retained in the mixed layer, the more likely it is that the C they contain will be respired back to CO\(_2\) and lost to the atmosphere rather than falling through the thermocline and accumulating in deep-water sediments. We do not believe that recycling is the only process responsible for producing this pattern. Indeed, such regularity is probably the product of many processes acting in concert (e.g., longer retention in the mixed layer, increasing total depth of the water column, decreasing terrestrial influence, etc.). Nevertheless, it is fully consonant with our conclusion that large lakes recycle nutrients more efficiently than small ones. The greater efficiency of nutrient recycling in the mixed layer in large than in small lakes has important implications for Fee's (1979) theory that the rate of nutrient recycling is a function of basin morphometry. He found that in small ELA lakes, the area of epilimnion sediments (\(A_e\)) divided by the volume of the epilimnion (\(V_e\)) was strongly correlated with rates of volumetric PP. He demonstrated that, if all other factors are equal, \(A_e/V_e\) is mathematically equivalent to the probability of retention of particles in the mixed layer and thus parameterized the rate of nutrient recycling. He cautioned that this might not be true in larger lakes, where processes that are negligible in small lakes could affect nutrient recycling. Our results bear out this prediction; as lakes increase in size, the increasing intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the increasing thickness of the mixed layer both retard sedimentation losses through the thermocline, thereby increasing mixed layer particle residence time. Consequently, a large lake with a low \(A_e/V_e\) value and a small lake with a high \(A_e/V_e\) value could have the same mixed layer particle residence times and similar rates of nutrient recycling. An important corollary is that large and small lakes with similar \(A_e/V_e\) values should respond differently to the same external P loading. Productivity should be higher in the large lake because of its higher rate of nutrient recycling. These results lend strong support to Margalef's (1974) theory that physical energy levels directly control food-web structures and the biogeochemical characteristics of water bodies. The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the water column of small lakes (Fig. 2 and 3); in contrast, large lakes had relatively well-mixed hypolimnia with maximum gradients at or just below the thermocline. This difference is probably the result of several processes: (1) Internal waves, which are the primary source of hypolimnetic turbulence, are significant only in lakes with surface areas >1000 ha (Boyce 1974); thus, in small lakes, nutrients from particles remineralized near the bottom of the water column move upward very slowly compared with larger lakes. (2) Sediment focussing is very important in small lakes (Anderson et al. 1987) and causes particles that fall through the thermocline to move rapidly to great depths. (3) Because small lakes have shallow mixed layers, significant quantities of light penetrate below their thermoclines (Fee et al. 1991), permitting large algal populations to develop deep in their water columns (Fee 1976). These algal populations intercept nutrients diffusing up from below and prevent them from reaching the thermocline. Schindler and Nighswander (1970) and Bayley et al. (1992) reported that precipitation was the major source of N and P to Canadian Shield lakes. However, their conclusion was based on results obtained from the study of quite small lakes. Our results (Fig. 6) indicate that this does not apply to Canadian Shield lakes >300 ha, where fluxes of N and P from terrestrial runoff and precipitation were very similar in magnitude. Unlike N and P, there was virtually no Si in precipitation, and mixing supplied substantial quantities of this nutrient only in very large lakes (Fig. 6). However, terrestrial runoff of Si was large, particularly in small and midsized lakes, and the sum of all the fluxes that we measured apparently match phytoplankton requirements. There must, therefore, be some reason, other than a lack of supply, for why diatoms are unimportant components of the summer phytoplankton community in small, stratified Canadian Shield lakes (Kling and Holmgren 1972; Findlay and Kasian 1990). Again, the most likely explanation is based on the low mixed-layer turbulence and shallow mixed-layer depths in small lakes. Theoretically, the higher specific gravity of diatoms gives them a selective advantage over nonsinking or weakly motile competitors because by sinking they increase the rate at which they contact dissolved nutrients (by thinning the nutrient-depleted boundary layer that surrounds them: Hutchinson 1967; Margalef 1974; Titman and Kilham 1976). This strategy works well in large lakes, where high turbulence and deep mixed layers keep cells from being rapidly lost by sedimentation through the thermocline. Diatoms are also well represented in small, unstratified lakes, which lack a hypolimnion sedimentation trap altogether (Kling and Holmgren 1972). However, this strategy apparently fails in small, stratified lakes where shallow mixed layers and relatively stable water columns lead to rapid removal of sinking cells from the mixed layer. Conclusion The increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size acted in concert with positive concentration gradients of NO\(_3^-\), TDN, and SRSi in the region of the thermocline to result in more of these nutrients being transported upwards through the thermoclines in large than in small lakes (Table 2). These nutrients, however, rarely limit phytoplankton growth in Canadian Shield lakes. Because concentration gradients of P, the nutrient that does limit algal growth in Canadian Shield lakes, were nil in the region of the thermocline in all of these lakes (Fig. 2 and 3; Table 2), upward fluxes of P were essentially zero in all lake sizes. Our results support Fee et al.'s (1992) hypothesis that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP. It does this by acting in concert with the increasing depth of the mixed layer to cause particles to be retained in the mixed layer longer, thus increasing the probability that nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than lost to the sediments. Our results do not, however, rule out the possibility that the greater rates of volumetric PP in midsized lakes reported by Fee et al. (1992) are caused by lake-to-lake differences of external P loading. That is, although our results show that, all other things being equal, higher turbulence and thicker mixed layers enhance nutrient recycling and lead to higher rates of areal PP in larger lakes, the approach we have taken of using runoff and precipitation data measured in the basin of one small ELA lake to estimate P loading in all the other lakes has inherent inaccuracies (Fee and Hecky 1992). External P loading within this lake-size series could vary enough to explain the observed differences of volumetric PP. Nevertheless, Fee et al. (1992) showed that it is unlikely that areal PP, which theoretically sets potential yields of higher trophic levels, is the result of lake-to-lake differences in external P loading. Our main conclusion, that the probability of regeneration of nutrients within the mixed layer increases with lake size, has an important corollary: external nutrient loads should be converted into higher trophic levels, including especially valued organisms such as fish, more efficiently in large than in small lakes. This prediction is in harmony with Nixon's (1988) conclusion that the greatest standing crops of benthos and highest fish yields come from the most energetic marine environments. He further noted that, as we found in large lakes, sediments from these highly productive regions contained less C than did sediments from less energetic environments. His interpretation of these observations was also the same as ours, viz., that energetic mixed layers recycle nutrients more efficiently than less energetic ones.
