Discussion

Seasonal and regional rates of sediment N transformations along the Texas coast—Results from experiments in Texas coastal systems show that N transformations were dynamic at the sediment–water interface but varied spatially and temporally in relative importance and magnitude (Tables 2–5). The most active processes, in terms of net flux magnitude, were NH\(_4^+\) production from the sediments, N fixation, and denitrification. Reactions involving NO\(_3^-\) and NO\(_2^-\) may have been dynamic, but their concentrations and net changes remained low during most experiments, indicating that they were static or in steady-state equilibrium. Mean sediment NH\(_4^+\) fluxes before and after isotope additions were positive or near zero at all sites except Sabine Lake in December 2000, which showed net NH\(_4^+\) uptake. Observed NH\(_4^+\) accumulation and measurement of potential DNRA rates suggest that DNRA was a major component of total NH\(_4^+\) production at some stations.

Benthic nutrient fluxes in nine Gulf of Mexico estuaries have been examined by several investigators and reviewed (Twilley et al. 1999). In agreement with results from other Gulf of Mexico estuaries (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994; Twilley et al. 1999), mean NH\(_4^+\) sediment regeneration rates (net fluxes) in the present study ranged from about 20 to 110 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Results for NO\(_3^-\) fluxes also follow patterns similar to previous results (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994) in Texas estuaries, except for Guadalupe Estuary, which exhibited high NH\(_4^+\) uptake (\( \sim 150 \) \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) and NO\(_3^-\) (plus

However, this observation may have been an exception to normal conditions as another study showed only moderate DIN fluxes in Guadalupe Estuary (Yoon and Benner 1992). Large spatial and temporal variations in N fluxes within and among estuaries make it difficult to discern patterns among them. For example, nutrient fluxes in Laguna Madre were lowest among estuaries examined in the earlier comparison (Twilley et al. 1999) but highest in the present comparison. The predominance of Texas brown tide in the 1990s may have affected this comparison. Dense populations of A. lagunensis remove NH₄⁺ from solution and keep concentrations low in the water (Gardner unpubl. data).

Sediment–atmosphere interactions: Is the sediment–water interface a site of net N₂ fixation (source) or net denitrification (sink) for available N?—Two approaches were taken to evaluate N fixation versus denitrification. First, net N₂ flux before \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition indicated whether atmospheric N₂ was a net source (N fixation) or sink (denitrification) of available N at the sediment–water interface. However, net changes do not reveal the extent to which N fixation and denitrification occur simultaneously. The isotope pairing approach (An et al. 2001) allows estimation of total rates for each process in the same cores but may not portray “actual rates” if the processes are affected by \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) addition.

In contrast to NH₄⁺ fluxes, which were almost always positive, net N₂ fluxes ranged from positive to negative values seasonally at the same sites and regionally among the sites. In Laguna Madre, net denitrification occurred on five occasions, net N fixation occurred twice, and zero net exchange occurred once. The opposite was observed in Sabine Lake, with N fixation dominating on six of seven occasions. In East Matagorda Bay, net N fixation was observed on 8 of 12 sampling occasions, but net rates were sometimes close to zero. Overall, net fixation was observed in the summer and winter (dry seasons) and net denitrification was observed in the spring and fall (wet seasons). Nitrogen fixation (Table 5) dominated in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay during April when O₂ levels were high in overlying waters (Fig. 4). However, denitrification dominated (Table 5) during summer when bottom water O₂ levels were low and the sulfide transition zone was near the sediment surface (Fig. 4). DNRA was six times higher at these sites in August than in April.

Denitrification rates from the present study were similar but, on average, higher than previous closed-chamber results in Texas estuaries (Yoon and Benner 1992; Zimmerman and Benner 1994). Underwater chamber results from Galveston Bay (An and Joye 2001) yielded higher denitrification rates than the present study and demonstrated that denitrification rates were higher in the light (mean N = 1000 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)) than in the dark (mean N = 480 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)).

Total N fixation versus denitrification rates, calculated in the enriched cores with the MIMS isotope pairing method, indicated that both processes proceeded simultaneously at comparable but different rates. For example, in Laguna Madre, mean postenrichment rates were 58 \( \pm \) 5 for N fixation, 32 \( \pm \) 5 for denitrification, and 41 \( \pm \) 13 for DNRA. Net N\(_2\) flux was 2.3 \( \pm \) 9.7 for the same cores before enrichment (excluding cores where enrichment experiments were not done). Unfortunately, \( ^{15} \)NO\(_3^-\) enrichments were not performed in April and August 1999 when highest net denitrification rates occurred. When these cores are included, net denitrification was dominant because of a large temporal effect. Results for both processes may be conservative since measurements did not account for N\(_2\)O production via incomplete denitrification. Also, both processes may be higher in natural light than dark or dim-light incubations because of labile organic matter production by photosynthesis (An and Joye 2001; An and Gardner 2002). Nitrogen fixation in Laguna Madre may have been underestimated since seagrasses were not included in experimental cores. Previous studies indicate that N fixation rates are high in seagrass beds where organic material is abundant (Paerl and Zehr 2000).

Data from the present study suggest that N fixation and denitrification are important and provide critical supply and removal mechanisms for available N in these productive systems. Although they occurred in both directions, net N\(_2\) fluxes across the sediment–water interface were comparable to NH\(_4^+\) fluxes and much higher than net NO\(_3^-\) or NO\(_2^-\) fluxes. This active exchange between atmospheric N\(_2\) and biotic N helps explain why Texas coastal systems have sufficient N

inputs to support high water-column N cycling rates, comparable to those in hypereutrophic ecosystems (Fig. 1), despite limited tributary nutrient inputs.

Relationship of DNRA to salinity and evidence for displacement of sediment-bound \( NH_4^+ \) by DNRA-produced \( NH_4^+ \)—Measuring N dynamics in sediment cores from a range of salinities provided an opportunity to examine relationships between N transformations and salinity and how they affect N removal or retention. Ammonium flux and DNRA rates increased with increasing salinity, but none of the other processes showed a significant salinity relationship. Denitrification: DNRA decreased significantly (\( p < 0.01 \)) with increasing salinity, suggesting that the fate of \( NO_3^- \) in surface sediments is related to salinity via DNRA and that DNRA is an important mechanism for retaining N in a biologically available form under saline conditions. DNRA also has been reported in other coastal systems (Koike and Hattori 1978; Sørensen 1978; Tobias et al. 2001). Enhancement of DNRA by sulfide- or sulfate-reducing bacteria (Rysgaard et al. 1996) is consistent (1) with the observed significant relationship between DNRA rates and salinity (with sulfate as a source) and (2) the large increase in DNRA rates observed when high sulfide concentrations, associated with low \( O_2 \), occurred near the sediment–water interface in Corpus Christi Bay (Fig. 4). The production of \( NH_4^+ \) by DNRA under conditions of high salinity may help explain why the Texas brown tide organism, A. lagunensis, which requires reduced N compounds as an N source, has thrived in the Laguna Madre Estuary when salinities were high (An and Gardner 2002). Aureoumbra lagunensis density in the estuary correlated directly with salinity at three stations sampled from July 1997 through October 1998 (Buskey et al. 2001).

Changes in total \( NH_4^+ \) release after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment were proportional to but greater (\( r = 0.9998, a = -12.3, b = 7.41, p < 0.01 \)) than DNRA rates when mean rates from Laguna Madre, Sabine Lake, and East Matagorda Bay were compared. These results imply that \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment may affect total \( NH_4^+ \) production, presumably via DNRA. The slope of this relationship indicates that increased \( NH_4^+ \) release stimulated by \( NO_3^- \) enrichment was about seven times the \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation fraction on average. However, this relationship did not hold if Corpus Christi Bay data were included, particularly in August 2002 when higher DNRA rates appeared to relate to reducing conditions rather than salinity.

Observed differences between the increases in total \( NH_4^+ \) release after enrichment versus \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation at normoxic stations indicates that rates estimated from the latter measurement may have underestimated potential DNRA. The \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) produced from \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) via DNRA may have exchanged with sediment-bound \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) (Rosenfeld 1979; Gardner et al. 1991; Seitzinger et al. 1991) as it diffused or migrated from the redox transition zone, where DNRA would occur, through the sediment to overlying water. If such exchange occurred, some \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) would have displaced \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) on sediment exchange sites and resulted in increased \( ^{14}NH_4^+ \) release from the sediments. This exchange would cause the measurement of released \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) in the overflowing water to underestimate potential DNRA resulting from the \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment when there is a zone of oxygenated sediments above the redox transition zone. The active exchange of \( NH_4^+ \) between the water and sediments, observed in the \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) addition experiment on East Matagorda Bay cores (Fig. 3), illustrates why increases in total \( NH_4^+ \) release were greater than \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) addition.

The migration distance to the overlying water for \( NH_4^+ \) formed from DNRA would be minimized where the water is hypoxic and the redox transition zone is at or near the sediment surface (e.g., August 2002, Corpus Christi Bay). This temporal difference in redox transition depth is illustrated by comparing mean \( O_2 \) and sulfide profiles for Corpus Christi Bay stations sampled in August 2002 versus April 2003 (Fig. 4). The mean transition depth was \( \sim 1 \) mm in August versus 28 mm in April. In agreement with this concept, there was no evidence for \( ^{15}NH_4^+ : ^{14}NH_4^+ \) isotope exchange reactions in the core experiments from August 2002 (i.e., mean total \( NH_4^+ \) release showed a slight decrease despite the presence of measurable \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \); Table 5). However, mean total \( NH_4^+ \) release increased after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment in April 2003 (Table 5) when \( O_2 \) and sulfide transition zones were deeper (Fig. 4).

Exchange reactions between free and bound \( NH_4^+ \) explain why measured \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) in outflow waters accounted for only a fraction of \( NO_3^- \) removal in isotope-addition experiments (An and Gardner 2002). A second possible sink for removed \( ^{15}NO_3^- \), which was not converted to \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \), is incomplete denitrification to \( N_2O \) and subsequent loss to the atmosphere (Smith et al. 1983). However, previous studies indicate that \( N_2O \) produced in estuarine sediments is small relative to \( N_2 \) (e.g., Seitzinger et al. 1983).

Evaluation of sediment–water N fluxes and transformations in Texas coastal systems offers insights about mechanisms controlling the sources and fate of available N in shallow, productive systems with variable and limited N inputs. Spatial and temporal similarities and differences in these processes among sites and seasons provides information about dominant cycling mechanisms and the importance of atmospheric \( N_2 \) as a source or sink for available N. The observed simultaneous N fixation and denitrification rates are consistent with the concept that available N compounds exchange actively with atmospheric \( N_2 \) and that N fixation is an important N source. Measurements of both processes were conservative since denitrification rates did not include \( N_2O \) production and assessments were not made under natural light or in the presence of seagrasses, conditions that would enhance production of labile organic compounds, which could serve as an energy source for N-transformation processes.

The observed relationship between sediment \( NH_4^+ \) release and salinity suggests that \( NH_4^+ \) regeneration increases with salinity. DNRA is an important process contributing to that trend. DNRA increased with salinity and was most important in Laguna Madre. DNRA also was important in southeastern Corpus Christi Bay during seasonal hypoxia. Comparison of potential DNRA rates estimated from \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation with those estimated from increased total \( NH_4^+ \) fluxes after \( ^{15}NO_3^- \) enrichment suggest that \( ^{15}NH_4^+ \) accumulation can underestimate potential DNRA in sediments under oxygenated waters.

</page>

<page number="9">

Overall, our results are consistent with the concepts that N fixation is important in Texas estuaries and that DNRA helps retain available N in hypersaline estuaries. They help explain why N cycling rates in Laguna Madre and other Texas estuaries resemble those for hypereutrophic systems even though tributary inputs are limited.

Deposition, mineralization, and storage of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern Great Barrier Reef shelf Daniel M. Alongi*, Lindsay A. Trott, John Pfitzner Australian Institute of Marine Science, PMB 3, Townsville MC, Qld. 4810, Australia Received 11 October 2006; received in revised form 10 July 2007; accepted 19 July 2007 Available online 1 August 2007 Abstract The flow of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern sections of the Great Barrier Reef continental shelf was examined. Most of the organic carbon (81–94%) and total nitrogen (74–92%) depositing to the seabed was mineralized, with burial of carbon (6–19%) and nitrogen (8–20%) being proportionally less on this tropical shelf compared with other non-deltaic shelves. Differences in carbon and nitrogen mineralization among stations related best to water depth and proximity to river basins, with rates of mineralization based on net \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production ranging from 17 to 39 (mean = 23) mmol C m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\). The overall ratio of O\(_2\):CO\(_2\) flux was 1.3, close to the Redfield ratio, implying that most organic matter mineralized was algal. Sulfate reduction was estimated to account for \( \approx 30\% \) (range: 6–62%), and denitrification for \( \approx 5\% \) (range: 2–13%), of total C mineralization; there was no measurable CH\(_4\) production. Discrepancies between \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production across the sediment–water interface and sediment incubations suggest that as much as 5 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (\( \approx 25\% \) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux) was involved in carbonate mineral formation. Most microbial activity was in the upper 20 cm of sediment. Rates of net NH\(_4^+\) production ranged from 1.6 to 2.7 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\), with highly variable N\(_2\) fixation rates contributing little to total N input. Ammonification and nitrification rates were sufficient to support rapid rates of denitrification (range: 0.1–12.4 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)). On average, nearly 50% of total N input to the shelf sediment was denitrified. The average rates of sedimentation, mineralization, and burial of C and N were greater in the northern section of the shelf than in the far northern section, presumably due to higher rainfall and river discharge, as plankton production was similar between regions. The relative proportion of plankton primary production remineralized at the seafloor was in the range of 30–50% which is at the high end of the range found on other shelves. The highly reactive nature of these sediments is attributed to the deposition of high-quality organic material as well as to the shallowness of the shelf, warm temperatures year-round, and a variety of physical disturbances (cyclones, trawling) fostering physicochemical conditions favorable for maintaining rapid rates of microbial metabolism. The rapid and highly efficient recycling of nutrients on the inner and middle shelf may help to explain why the coral reefs on the outer shelf have remained unscathed from increased sediment delivery since European settlement. Introduction There is considerable concern about the impact and fate of terrestrially derived material entering the continental shelf of the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area (GBRWHA). Reduction in coral growth and a shift in the relative abundance and composition of corals and algae of nearshore fringing reefs, especially in inner shelf areas adjacent to intensively cultivated catchments, have been attributed to elevated availability of nutrients and suspended sediment loads (Fabricius et al., 2003). Intensification of land use and subsequent erosion of grazing land and crop land have resulted in an increase in sediment and nutrient delivery to the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) since the mid-1880s (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The magnitude of the increase is unclear, but more than one-half of sediment loading is estimated to come from grazing land, with 10% from crop land, and the remainder from natural erosion (Neil et al., 2002). Total sediment delivery is estimated at about 7 Mt y\(^{-1}\), with enhanced delivery possibly as high as 14–28 Mt y\(^{-1}\) (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The most intensive cultivation, and presumably the most intensive runoff, occurs in the latitudinal band of 16–18°S in the northern section of the GBRWHA. Less enhanced runoff occurs adjacent to less populated and cultivated catchments in the far northern section of the shelf. Nutrient cycling and inorganic and organic carbon dynamics is poorly understood on the GBR shelf, as most focus has been on cycling of elements on individual reefs rather than on non-reefal regions of the shelf. A number of studies have measured concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients along the length of the GBR, with data indicating concentrations typical of tropical waters under calm conditions, but elevated concentrations during periods of sustained winds when sediments are re-suspended, and during wet season plumes. GBR waters are characterized by N:P ratios of particulate matter of 8:1 and dissolved N:P ratios of 14:1 (Furnas, 2003). These low ratios likely reflect P adsorption onto inorganic particles, but may possibly indicate material of good nutritive value (Furnas et al., 1995). Sedimentation fluxes (based on data from sediment traps; Furnas et al., 1995) have been difficult to obtain in such shallow waters as most material recovered appears to be re-suspended matter, mucus, and other colloidal material. Stoichiometric ratios vary widely, but suggest fairly labile material settling to the seabed. Nutrient cycling in non-reefal GBR sediments is not well characterized, although several studies have pointed to \( \mu \)M concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients in interstitial water and rapid microbial activity (Alongi, 1989; Lourey et al., 2001). High rates of benthic microbial activity and lack of vertical profiles of dissolved and particulate nutrient concentrations suggest little burial of reactive organic matter, in agreement with low burial rates measured in the central GBR (Brunskill et al., 2002). The physical and biological complexity of the GBR limits the application of results from one section of the shelf to another. The GBR province is the exemplar of a carbonate rimmed shelf, and is one of the world’s largest continental margins with extensive mixed terrigenous–carbonate sedimentary facies (Hopley et al., 2007). The GBR shelf is a passive continental margin with a low seafloor gradient of <1:1000. The development and tectonic setting of this shelf is well understood compared with other tropical continental shelves. The shelf is wide (30–150 km) and shallow (<80 m at shelf break), encompassing an area of 225,000 km\(^2\), and is uniquely rimmed on the outer shelf margin by nearly 2500 individual coral reefs comprising the GBR, which stretches over 2000 km (10–24°S) parallel to the Queensland coast (Maxwell, 1968). The GBR shelf shares some characteristics with other tropical shelves, such as (1) a benthic fauna dominated by large epibenthos (e.g., echinoderms), lancelets, and large Foraminifera; (2) infaunal communities composed mostly of pioneering, small opportunists that surface deposit—and/or suspension feed; (3) abundant demersal assemblages, especially crustaceans; (4) intermittent intrusions of upwelled, nutrient-rich water; and (5) a summer wet season in which cyclones and monsoonal rains occur. The shallowness of the shelf in concert with severe summer weather, extensive trawling, and erratic nutrient inputs fosters plankton and benthic communities adapted to respond quickly to such disturbances and fluctuating rates of food supply. A sharp, across-shelf gradient of sedimentary facies from inshore terrigenous mud and quartz sand to mixed terrigenous–carbonate deposits mid-shelf to impure and pure carbonate within and between reefs on the outer margin is the dominant geological characteristic of the shelf (Hopley et al., 2007). In the far northern (Fig. 1a) and northern (Fig. 1b) sectors, this gradient narrows but persists from the south. On the inner shelf, the seaward limit Fig. 1. Depth contours are in meters. of the coastal zone is dynamic, varying in time and space and formed when turbid inshore and estuarine waters mix and are trapped along the coast; the coastal boundary breaks down under strong winds and river discharge (Wolanski and Ridd, 1990). River floods typically last for a few days and enter the shelf as plumes mostly in summer; runoff is negligible the rest of the year. Coastal boundary zones often form in bays sheltered by capes and headlands. Coastal waters move slowly longshore towards the headlands but may be periodically diverted as an ebb tidal jet peeling off from the headland, presumably enriching the middle shelf. Neither eddies formed by the rugged coastline nor longshore currents formed by the southeast trades can propagate in sheltered waters due to friction. Within the coastal boundary layer, dispersion of nutrients and particulate matter is by tidal diffusion only, especially when winds are light. It is for this reason that there is constant exchange between estuaries and the coastal boundary layer, but much slower rates of mixing between inshore and offshore waters (Wolanski, 1994). The phenomenon of trapping due to friction and the presence of coastal boundary zones ensure that most terrigenous sediment persists as a narrow band along the inner shelf. The regional distribution of Holocene terrigenous deposits and the sharp across-shelf gradient from terrigenous to carbonate facies have been well described (Maxwell, 1968; Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004; Hopley et al., 2007). Evidence from X-radiographs and radionuclide profiles shows that episodes of re-suspension, re-deposition, and intense reworking of surface deposits are common on the inner shelf (Alongi and Christoffersen, 1992; Brunskill et al., 2002). The sediment-starved middle shelf is a zone of transitional (30–60% carbonate) and impure (60–80% CaCO₃) carbonate facies. Surface water speeds commonly reach 50 cm s⁻¹ or more, but do not cause significant bedload transport. A recent analysis (Larcombe and Carter, 2004) has argued that cyclones transport post-storm mud drapes on top of the sandy middle shelf bed that are fully remixed into the sand facies by persistent bioturbation. Along shelf, cyclone-driven flow produces shelf-parallel, bed-sediment transport that is delimited as dunes, ribbons, or small dune areas on the middle shelf. Such strong flows (up to 130–200 cm s\(^{-1}\)) have resulted in erosion of Pleistocene deposits that are often exposed beneath a veneer of muddy sand and unconsolidated shell. This veneer, the net sedimentation of \( \approx 10,000 \) y of seabed exposure, is continually eroded and re-suspended by cyclones; mud in suspension is transported northwards along shelf and advected landwards. The result is dunes and ribbons of bioclastic deposits up to \( \approx 15 \) cm thick on the middle shelf (Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004). It is on this portion of the shelf that epibenthic communities are most abundant and diverse, dominated by echinoderms, bryozoans, large ascidians, sponges, and Foraminifera (Alongi, 1989). In this paper, we detail studies of benthic metabolic rates and pathways of carbon and nitrogen cycling at inner and middle shelf sites proximal to impacted catchments on the northern GBR and to less heavily impacted catchments on the far northern GBR shelf. Some first-order calculations are also made to understand the benthic contribution to nutrient dynamics on these sections of the shelf and how (or if) they differ to earlier studies in the central section of the GBR shelf. 2. On the first two cruises, sediment cores to a maximum penetration depth of 20 cm were taken using a modified 0.027 m\(^2\) Bouma boxcorer. On the last three cruises, boxcorer samples were taken for flux measurements across the sediment–water interface (see below), and 1-m length cores were taken using a Kasten corer and were handled as described in Brunskill et al. (2002). 2.2. Sediment granulometry and solid-phase elements Boxcorer and Kasten corer samples were used for analysis of sediment grain size and percent sand, silt, and clay using the standardized procedure of Folk (1974) on an automated particle size counter. Sediments were classified as mud, sand, sandy mud, or muddy sand, based on the definitions in Folk (1974). Further sub-samples from the boxcores were taken at 2-cm intervals to a depth of 20 cm on the first two cruises and at 15–20 irregularly spaced intervals to a depth of 1 m on the last three cruises. These sub-samples were frozen at sea, then thawed and wet and dry weighted to determine water content, and ground to a fine powder for determination of total carbon and total nitrogen on a Perkin-Elmer 2400 CHNS/O Series II analyzer and for total organic carbon on a Shimadzu TOC analyzer with solid sampler. Other elements (P, S, Mn, Fe) were determined after strong acid digestion on a Varian Liberty inductively coupled atomic emission spectrometer following the procedure of Loring and Rantala (1992). Total inorganic carbon was assumed as CaCO₃, and was determined by difference between the total carbon and total organic carbon concentrations. 2.3. Mass sediment accumulation Mass sediment accumulation rates (MAR) were determined from gamma spectrometric measurements of \(^{210}\mathrm{Pb}\), \(^{137}\mathrm{Cs}\), and other radionuclides made on sequentially sliced duplicate 100-cm-long cores taken using the Kasten corer (Brunskill et al., 2002). Each core was cut into 2-cm slices from the sediment surface to 20-cm depth, then into 4-cm slices to the bottom of the core. Gamma ray measurements were made on 50–150 g dried and ground sediment from each slice packed by a 10 metric ton hydraulic press into a custom designed gas-tight plastic container. Four Canberra GL2020R/S special low-energy, low-background planar germanium detectors housed inside 10-cm thick, lead-walled castles with steel liners were used to collect the gamma photons. Energy spectra were calibrated with standards consisting of known low-activity spikes of suitable nuclides from Amersham and CANMET calibrated sources in silica sand and sand/calcium carbonate matrices. Minimum detection limits, in Bq kg⁻¹ dry weight of sediment, for a 50 g sample counted for 1 d are 4 for \(^{210}\mathrm{Pb}\), 0.5 for \(^{226}\mathrm{Ra}\), 1.0 for \(^{228}\mathrm{Ra}\), 0.5 for \(^{228}\mathrm{Th}\), 1.5 for \(^{234}\mathrm{Th}\), and 0.7 for \(^{137}\mathrm{Cs}\). Interpretations of the radiochemical profiles were done with several sub-models incorporating weighted least-squares regression analysis (Robbins, 1978, 1979). Sediment mass accumulation rates (MAR) were multiplied by average TOC and TN sediment concentrations in the same cores to provide estimates of accumulation of these elements. 2.4. Solute fluxes Solute fluxes across the sediment–water interface were measured using three sets of three closed opaque chambers (volume: 1 l; area: 82 cm²) from which \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \), O₂, and dissolved inorganic nutrient and metal samples were taken at 3 h intervals for 12–18 h. Two chambers were gently placed into each of three boxcorer samples (\( n = 9 \); total area = 738 cm²), which were incubated in the dark in a running seawater bath to maintain ambient seawater temperature. Each chamber had a propeller-electric motor unit and two sampling ports on opposite sides of the chamber (Alongi et al., 2006). Small replicate chambers were used to determine the extent of small-scale variability between replicate boxcores and to ensure adherence to the assumptions for analysis of variance (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Dissolved oxygen was measured using an O₂ probe (TPS™ Model WP-82 DO meters) placed into one sampling port; the other port was fitted with plastic tubing to draw off 10 ml samples for \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and dissolved nutrients and metals. The samples for \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and dissolved inorganic nutrients were filtered (0.45 μm Minisart® filters) and either kept cool and dark (\( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \)) or frozen until analysis. Concentrations of NH₄⁺, NO₂⁻ + NO₃⁻, and PO₄³⁻ were determined using automated techniques (Ryle et al., 1981; Ryle and Wellington, 1982). Concentrations of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) were determined using the procedure of Hall and Aller (1992). Dissolved metals were analyzed as detailed in Section 2.6. 2.5. Sulfate reduction Rates of sulfate reduction were measured in triplicate 2.7-cm diameter plastic cores taken to a depth of 20 cm from boxcores on the first three cruises. Cores were injected at 2-cm intervals with carrier-free \(^{35}\mathrm{SO}_4\) (Fossing and Jorgensen, 1989), incubated for 6–9 h, and then terminated by fixing sediments in 20% zinc acetate. On the last two cruises, triplicate 2.7-cm plastic cores were taken horizontally from Kasten cores at 0–2 cm and at various intervals to 1 m. The samples were capped at both ends and the middle 2 cm of each sample was injected and processed as described above. Samples were then frozen until a two-step distillation procedure was used to determine the fraction of reduced radiolabel shunted into the acid-volatile sulfide (AVS) and chromium-reducible sulfur (CRS) pools. 2.6. Net metal, \( \sum CO_2 \), and \( NH_4^+ \) production Rates of net production of dissolved metals, \( \sum CO_2 \), and \( NH_4^+ \) from sediments at each site were measured by incubating two sets of duplicate sediment cores taken from boxcores on the first three cruises, and from sub-samples taken from Kasten cores on the last two cruises (Alongi et al., 2006). From the boxcores, one entire set of 20-cm length cores were incubated, mixed, and placed in large opaque glass bottles for 6 d in a N_2-filled glove bag, to give integrated rates over the top 20 cm. The other set of cores was sliced immediately at 4-cm intervals and each sediment cake was placed into separate plastic cassettes containing a 0.4 \( \mu \)m Poretics\textregistered{} filter and squeezed on a pore water extractor under gentle N_2 pressure. Each sample was first squeezed for \( \sum CO_2 \) and metals, then each sample was mixed in 1 M KCl solution and after 2–3 h squeezed again to obtain total extractable \( NH_4^+ \). The whole cores incubated for 6 d were processed by taking sub-samples and upscaling reaction rates to the entire sediment volume. From the Kasten cores, separate sets of samples were taken at various depth intervals, incubated in sealed opaque glass jars at in situ temperature in a water bath for 6–10 d, and processed as described above. Samples were processed for \( \sum CO_2 \) and dissolved inorganic nutrients as described earlier, and pore water Cl\(^-\), S, Fe, Ca, Mg, Sr, and Mn were analyzed on the Varian ICP-MS. pH was measured from the Kasten cores using a Model PBFC pH electrode which was allowed to equilibrate for 10–15 min before readings were taken on a TPS LC 80 meter. The pH electrode was calibrated using 6.00, 7.00, and 8.00 NIST standards. Saturation states for calcite and aragonite were calculated using the formula, \( \Omega_{CALITE, ARAGONITE} = [Ca^{2+}][CO_3^{2-}]/K_{CALCITE, ARAGONITE} \), in which the apparent solubility products for calcite (\( K_{CALCITE} \)) and aragonite (\( K_{ARAGONITE} \)) fit to temperature and salinity by Mucci (1983) were used (Millero, 1995). The carbonate concentration was calculated from the pH and \( \sum CO_2 \) data in estimating the second apparent dissociation constant of carbonic acid at the appropriate temperature and salinity (Mehrbach et al., 1973; Millero, 1995). 2.7. Nitrification, denitrification, and nitrogen fixation Nitrification was estimated using the acetylene inhibition technique (Sloth et al., 1992). Six opaque chambers were inserted into boxcorer samples as for the other solute flux measurements and incubated identically, except that three chambers immediately received 50 ml of acetylene-saturated seawater to inhibit nitrification. Sediment–water fluxes of NH_4\(^+\) were measured in both sets of chambers. The difference in the slope of NH_4\(^+\) vs. time between the treatments was assumed to correspond to the rate of nitrification. Denitrification was measured from replicate sediment samples taken from boxcores using the N_2-gas flux technique (Nowicki, 1994). Fluxes of CH_4 were measured in the same chambers. Open-ended bottles were carefully pushed 8–10 cm into the sediment (volume: 230–385 cm\(^3\)) and samples were kept at ambient temperature in an aerated running seawater bath until return to the laboratory. Any obvious surface fauna was removed with tweezers before each sample was extruded into a gas-tight glass chamber (height = 23.5 cm; i.d. = 7.6 cm). Sediments in each chamber were covered with seawater sparged with either 80%He/20%O_2 mixture (four experimental chambers per site) or 100% He (one to two control chambers per site) to remove N_2 and, in the case of the experimental cores, to maintain dissolved O_2 concentrations. The overlying water in each sealed chamber was stirred continuously. All chambers were incubated for 9 d in the dark at ambient temperatures. In the experimental chambers, the gas phase was flushed every 8 h for the first 2 d with a 80% He/20% O_2 mixture, and again the water overlying the sediment was periodically replaced with low-N_2 seawater after 3 d. The control chambers were treated similarly but incubated under anoxic conditions to block nitrification and denitrification. A 100% He-flushed, low-N_2 seawater exchange was carried out after 3 d, wherein all control and experimental chambers were sealed and gas samples were withdrawn for measurement of gas concentrations in the headspace. The accumulation of N_2 and O_2 in the headspace was measured each day for the next 5 d using an MTI Analytical Instruments P200 gas chromatograph. Calibration standards were run with each set of samples using a certified gas mixture. Background de-gassing of N_2 from the control chambers was subtracted from the total N_2 flux measured in the experimental chambers to derive the rate of N_2 flux due to denitrification (Nowicki, 1994). Denitrification rates were calculated as the average rate of triplicate cores from each site, from 3 to 4 individual incubation periods. CH_4 accumulation rates in the gas headspaces were considered de novo synthesis and were calculated as the average rate of triplicate cores from each site using oxic chambers only. Nitrogen fixation in sediments at each site was measured in three to four dark and clear chambers using the acetylene reduction technique (Capone, 1993). Samples were taken by inserting open-ended chambers (surface area: 64 cm^2) into the sediment to a depth of 5 cm. The chambers and soil plugs were then gently withdrawn with minimal disturbance. The bases of the chambers were sealed with PVC caps containing an inert rubber plate. A 10% acetylene/air mixture was created (sediment volume: 320 cm^3), added in the water phase, and the headspace was sampled immediately and at 3 h intervals, with a final sampling at \( \approx 20 \) h. Acetylene and ethylene were analyzed simultaneously by gas chromatography. The ethylene rates were converted to rates of N_2 fixation using the theoretical factor of 4 C_2H_2 molecules equalling 1 N molecule (Capone, 1993). 3. Results 3.1. Sediment accumulation The excess \(^{210}\)Pb profiles and inventories alone allowed a reasonably consistent estimation of sediment accumulation rate at each station (Table 4). At Sta. HAY, the entire \(^{210}\)Pb inventory was captured within the upper 15–20 cm of sediment. Cores 3582 and 3583 had different mixed layers of 6 and 2 cm, respectively, but similar excess \(^{210}\)Pb inventories (Table 4). In core 3583 (Fig. 3), \(^{137}\)Cs was located in the section of the sediment profile where it would be expected to be found from \(^{137}\)Cs bomb fallout history (1958–1980) (Pfitzner et al., 2004) and therefore provided good support for the sedimentation rate derived from the excess \(^{210}\)Pb profile. Averaging both Sta. HAY cores, excess \(^{210}\)Pb-derived mass sediment accumulation was 1.55 kg sediment m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\). At Sta. HAN, an MAR could be derived only from core 3585 (Table 4) as core 3584 appeared to have suffered scouring and rapid re-deposition of material. Cores 3580 and 3581 from Sta. BUK differed in their radiochemical profiles, with core 3581 indicating a deeper mixed layer and lower MAR (Table 4). Both cores showed variable down-core changes in \(^{238}\)U and \(^{40}\)K (data not shown) suggesting that sediment may have been derived from different sources. At Sta. PCB, core 3570 indicated a thick (17 cm) mixed layer, which was partly supported by the \(^{137}\)Cs profile. However, the \(^{137}\)Cs penetrated deeper into the core than the excess \(^{210}\)Pb, suggesting materials of different origin. Core 3571 indicated a deeper unmixed profile of radionuclides, a thinner mixed layer, but a similar MAR. Averaging both cores, the MAR at Sta. PCB was 2.5 kg sediment m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\). This average is less than the value derived from the earlier work at this site by Torgersen et al. (1983), but the high MAR of core 3571 equivalent to a deposition rate of 5.9 mm y\(^{-1}\) equates well with the deposition rate of 6.07 mm y\(^{-1}\) measured in 1980. In the northern section of the GBR shelf, most cores indicated higher rates of MAR than in the far northern section (Table 4). At Sta. LOW, core 3578 showed an excellent excess \(^{210}\)Pb profile supported by a small amount of \(^{137}\)Cs in the upper section of the core; core 3579 indicated a similar mixed layer thickness (8–9 cm) but a stepped excess \(^{210}\)Pb profile, which may have been due to several episodes of deposition. Our data indicate that the patterns of organic carbon mineralization relate best to distance from the coast (expressed as water depth in the statistical analyses) and proximity to river basins, rather than simple geography. There were no clear differences in rates of planktonic primary production between the far northern and northern sectors of the shelf (M. Furnas, pers. comm.). The high mineralization efficiencies (81–94%; average: 89%) translate into low burial efficiencies (6–19%; average \( \approx 11\%\)). It is likely that the true burial rates are lower. The radiochemical profiles resulted in model estimates of sedimentation ranging from 1.4 to 5.8 kg m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\) and our results agree well with earlier data from Princess Charlotte Bay and off Cairns (Torgersen et al., 1983; Brady et al., 1994). However, storms and other physical disturbances, such as trawling, result in a fining upwards of sediment. Experiments with GBR sediments mimicking these disturbances found that the net result of an increase in the proportion of fine particles toward the sediment–water interface may incorrectly suggest recent increases in sedimentation (Towler and Smith, 2000). Some of our radionuclide profiles (e.g., Sta. HIG) showed some evidence of episodes of large slabs of sediment depositing, as well as scouring of seabed. The most likely explanation for these low burial rates is the fact that the GBR shelf is shallow, warm year-round, and therefore subject to intense disturbance of the sediment surface and sediment mixing by cyclones, storms, and trawling. This idea is supported by the vertical distribution of benthic infauna and X-radiographic evidence of sediments further south near Hinchinbrook Island (Alongi and Christoffersen, 1992). Most infauna are small sized, of low abundance, and living predominantly in the upper 2–5 cm, but large, deep-dwelling equilibrium species are rare. X-radiographs consistently show that the sedimentary fabric consists of shell-gravel bands and cross-bedding features attributable to episodes of erosion. Much of the inner and middle shelf is above the mean shoaling depth for wind waves and tidal scouring. When spring tides (up to 3.8 m) coincide with low intervals of sea level (which oscillates in this region up to 35 cm), cycles of erosion, re-suspension, and deposition occur. Such events can occur several times a year as they may not be solely dependent on astronomical tides (Wolanski and Ridd, 1990; Wolanski, 1994). As most carbon remineralization occurs in the upper sediment layers, most decomposition is likely to have been accomplished by aerobic bacteria as many of the attributes of these sites, including fully oxic conditions in the bottom water, rapid water currents, a significant sand fraction, and high rates of surface sediment disturbance, may promote extensive aerobic respiration. The exceptions to this caveat are Stas. PCB and CNS, which were composed of fine-grained terrigenous silt and clay particles having the highest Fe and Mn concentrations. The \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) uptake rates were high (range: 12–63 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\); average \( \approx 25 \)) compared to other shelves (Canfield, 1993; Henrichs, 1993; Aller et al., 1996; Canfield et al., 2005; Emerson and Hedges, 2006) but very similar to rates measured further north in the Gulf of Papua (average \( \approx 23 \) mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\); Aller et al., 2004). Aerobic respiration cannot be readily separated from possible manganese and iron reduction, but several pieces of evidence imply that metal reduction may be a minor proportion of total carbon oxidation at these sites. First, large relative contributions from metal reducers are ordinarily found in fine-grained terrigenous deposits, where high content of diagenetically active iron and manganese oxides, well-oxygenated bottom water, and a moderately high input of reactive organic matter support a large bioturbating infauna (Canfield et al., 2005). In the GBR, total solid-phase Fe and Mn concentrations and reactivity are low (Alongi et al., 1993), and although inputs of reactive organic matter are high, the infauna, as discussed above, are small sized and live primarily within the upper 2–5 cm; there are rarely any infaunal organisms that build deep tubes or burrows. Physical disturbances are common, but mostly restricted to the upper sediment deposits. X-radiographs from most of our sites rarely indicated any significant biogenic structures beneath the surface layers. So, continuous reworking by infauna is unlikely to be a significant mechanism to replenish the supply of metal oxides to support metal reduction. Second, although some oxidation likely occurred upon sample handling, some nitrate was found in the pore water beneath the sediment surface; measurable Fe reduction normally does not occur within zones of significant NO\(_3^-\) concentrations (Walter and Burton, 1990). Third, evidence from other studies suggests that Mn reduction is insignificant except at sites with unusually high Mn oxide concentrations, and in certain intertidal habitats where plant roots and bioturbating fauna can reoxidize Mn (and Fe) oxides (Canfield et al., 2005, Table 5.8). Finally, we did not measure any net production of dissolved Mn or Fe either in surface sediment incubations or across the sediment–water interface. Excluding Stas. PCB and CNS, all of the other stations were either sandy or calcareous or both, implying insufficient reactive metal oxides necessary for Fe or Mn reduction. In adjacent sites on Sudbury and Arlington Reefs (Alongi et al., 2006), no evidence of Fe or Mn reduction was found, in agreement with earlier studies that have indicated unsuitable conditions for metal reduction in carbonate-rich, metal-poor deposits (Walter et al., 1993). The potentially significant role of aerobic respiration in these sediments is in agreement with measurements made in other carbonate-dominated sediments (Boucher et al., 1994; Werner et al., 2006). Episodes of re-suspension and deposition may foster aerobic pathways by recharging the dissolved oxygen supply in surface sediments. The differences between the diffusive fluxes (average = 16.6 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) and production fluxes (average = 21.6 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) indicate either that a moderate amount (\( \approx 5 \) mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) of remineralized \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) is involved in authigenic mineral formation or that transport-reaction processes are not in steady state. Most of the imbalances in \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux were <10% of total C remineralization, well within the systematic error of many of the multiple methods used. No net fluxes of Ca, Fe, or Mn were measured across the sediment–water interface at any of the stations. The rates of DIC generated in the subsurface sediment incubations are not in balance with the amounts of Ca, Mg, and Sr calculated to precipitate in the deeper sediments, but the relationship between sulfate reduction and carbonate mineral kinetics is complex and non-linear, with aragonite supersaturation occurring at both low and high rates of sulfate reduction (Walter and Burton, 1990), and such may be the case in the GBR deposits. The rates of sulfate reduction were similar to those measured in other regions of the GBR shelf (Alongi, 1992; Alongi et al., 2006), and accounted for 6–62% of total carbon mineralization. Most radiolabel was shunted into the CRS fraction and although sulfate reduction was measurable to 1 m at some locations, most activity was confined to surficial sediments. The diminished role of sulfate reduction at some locations is consistent with low S content of sediment and C:S ratios (range: 2.7–5.5) generally higher than in normal marine shelf sediments (Canfield et al., 2005). Although not as dramatic, this pattern is similar to that found in tropical deltaic sediments off the Amazon and Fly Rivers (Aller et al., 1996, 2004). In this study, C:S ratios correlated with rates of sulfate reduction, and the lack of sulfides detected in the pore water suggests that there is comparatively little preservation of S (or Fe) as stable sulfide minerals. Total carbon oxidation rates did not correlate with sedimentation rate. The lack of a significant correlation suggests that other factors such as mixing/physical disturbance and the narrow seasonal range of water temperature play an important role in influencing rates of total carbon oxidation. Empirical and modelling studies have shown that re-suspension of surface sediments stimulates mineralization by aerating sediments, mixing labile organic matter, and by stimulating bacterial growth and minimizing preservation of carbon (Wainwright and Hopkinson, 1997; Aller and Aller, 2004). In a shallow water column, a tight coupling is likely between benthic and pelagic mineralization and nutrient turnover (Alongi and McKinnon, 2005). This scenario is similar to that suggested by Aller (1998, 2004) for mobile shelf muds which appear to act as suboxic, fluidized bed reactors. Comparison of benthic carbon oxidation with pelagic primary production (M. Furnas, pers. comm.) indicates that the relative proportion of water-column organic carbon production remineralized in GBR sediments is in the range of 30–50% which is slightly higher than the range found in other shelf environments (Gattuso et al., 1998). Benthic microalgal production also contributes to benthic remineralization, as seagrass beds were found, but primary production was not measured, at several stations. Terrestrial C input also contributes to benthic carbon oxidation. Using floating sediment traps, Furnas (per. comm.) measured rates of organic carbon sedimentation greater than 3 × benthic mineralization rates. Most of this material was re-suspended sediment, but nearly a third was flocculent or colloidal aggregates, perhaps formed as a result of microbial mediation and exudation of extracellular by-products, as described by Fabricius et al. (2003) in the GBR. Rapid rates of plankton activity within a persistent coastal boundary layer, coupled with warm temperatures, and intermittent mixing and re-suspension, may foster the production of such material. In subtropical and tropical waters, bacteria, protozoa, microflagellates, and appendicularians are known to exude mucopolysaccharides that may promote colloidal formation (Hansen et al., 1996). The overall ratio of O_2:CO_2 fluxes was 1.3, based on the slope of the regression of the two solutes (Fig. 5). This value is very close to the Redfield ratio, implying that reoxidation of reduced solutes approximated their production, supporting the lack of burial of a significant proportion of the reduced metabolites. There was likely some production of benthic microalgal and seagrass carbon at these locations, given the high water clarity and shallow depths, but respiration quotients are sometimes > 1; for instance, use of model Redfield ratio organic matter C_{106}H_{260}O_{106}N_{16}P_{1} and average marine plankton C_{106}H_{177}O_{37}N_{17}S_{0.4}P_{1} yields respiration coefficients for complete oxidation of 1.3 and 1.45, respectively (Middelburg et al., 2005). 4.2. Nitrogen dynamics The ratio of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 : \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) production in these sediments (Table 7) is somewhat greater than the C:N ratio of particulate material found in the sediment traps. Furnas (per. comm.) measured an average C:N ratio of 8:1 in Princess Charlotte Bay, 7:1 in waters near Sta. HIG, FIZ, and RUS, and 5:1 off Cairns. These differences between benthic and pelagic C:N ratios likely reflect the differences in the composition of the organic material and the types of bacterial assemblages in the traps and in the sediments. Given the number of different methods used and process measurements taken, our data are reasonable to the extent that the sediment C and N budgets are in overall balance. Like carbon burial, nitrogen burial may be overestimated, although any buried N is likely to be refractory material such as fulvic and humic complexes. Rates of nitrogen fixation were patchy but, on average, a small contribution to total N input as in other marine sediments (Canfield et al., 2005). Our rates were within the range of those measured in reef sediments, including those of the GBR (Capone et al., 1992; Charpy-Roubaud et al., 2001; Kayanne et al., 2005; Alongi et al., 2006). The patchiness of nitrogen-fixing activity corresponds to the patchiness of algal mats on the GBR lagoon floor (Alongi and McKinnon, 2005). Rates of net NH_4^+ release, a proxy measure of ammonification, were rapid as were rates of nitrification. The good match between measurements suggests a tight link between nitrogen transformation processes; any discrepancies may be due to unmeasured DON pools and fluxes, and systematic error as a result of our use of small chambers. Most nitrogen transformation activity appears to have taken place in surface sediments at most of the stations with some, but little activity, below the upper 20 cm. Most of the measurements of NO_2^- + NO_3^- flux across the sediment–water interface indicate sediment uptake rather than release. The mineralization and transformation of N appears to have been rapid enough to support the measured rates of denitrification. Sediment pH was near optimal for nitrification as most nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas grow best at near neutral pH (Canfield et al., 2005). Free sulfide, which can completely inactivate nitrifiers, was absent. Further, water temperatures were within the temperature optimum for typical mesophilic nitrifiers. The denitrification rates were high to the extent that, on average, nearly half of the input of N to the sediment was denitrified (Table 8). These percentages are at the high end of the range of values estimated from unpolluted temperate shelves and estuaries (Seitzinger, 1988; Canfield et al., 2005), but similar to that estimated by Aller et al. (1996) for off the Amazon. Based on sediment incubations and pore water distributions, Aller et al. (1996) suggested the potential for Amazon shelf sediments to denitrify \( \approx 100\% \) of remineralized NH_4^+, while shelf-scale models and budgets indicate that > 50% of recycled inorganic N from the seabed is lost to the atmosphere. Alongi (1990) earlier hypothesized that tropical shelves may be especially important sites of denitrification in a global context because of shelf-edge upwelling, enhanced monsoonal runoff from land, and the suboxic nature of sediment deposits. Such appears to be the case also for the GBR shelf. Denitrification may be enhanced by the lack of sulfides and mineral sulfide formation in these sediments, as denitrifying bacteria are inhibited by sulfides and sulfate-reducing activity. Other factors that drive denitrification, such as temperature, bioturbation, and the supply of organic matter, were within optimal limits, based on laboratory studies of denitrification and the growth of denitrifying bacteria (cf. Canfield et al., 2005). Few comparative data are available for mineralization and burial efficiencies, especially for nitrogen in marine sediments. What data are available indicate that <10% of N is typically buried in marine deposits (Canfield et al., 2005). Burial of N in these GBR sediments averaged \( \approx 11\% \), presumably mostly refractory material. These values may be lower, and the N mineralization efficiencies higher, given the likelihood that burial is overestimated, as discussed earlier. N burial in carbonate muds of nearby Arlington and Sudbury Reefs were similar, averaging 10% and 7% of total N input, respectively (Alongi et al., 2006). Using a mass balance approach, Brunskill et al. (2002) estimated that about 1% of river and marine organic carbon was preserved on the central section of the GBR shelf, but that 3% of river and mangrove organic carbon was buried in intertidal and very shallow-water sediments. In any case, the data indicate that the vast bulk of labile nitrogen is mineralized rapidly throughout the GBR. 4.3. Regional differences In the far northern GBR, a decline in organic matter input was observed with distance from the Normanby River, underscoring the importance of river discharge to nutrient dynamics on this section of the shelf. The inverse correlations of water depth (distance from land) with nitrogen mineralization and total carbon and nitrogen input support this observation. In the northern section of the shelf, a similar situation exists with the two stations nearest to river mouths (Stas. CNS and RUS) having the highest rates of C input. Stas. FIZ and HIG presumably are draped by plumes in the wet season from the Russell/Mulgrave Rivers, yet this area is open to the SE trade winds and longshore currents. Wolanski et al. (2005) observed large-scale resuspension in this area, with the reefs fringing High Island accumulating large slugs of this re-suspended sediment during summer storms. Our measured rates of benthic nutrient regeneration and concentrations of pore water N solutes are well within the range of measurements made in 1992–1993 (Lourey et al., 2001) indicating no clear change over the past decade. The patterns of benthic nutrient dynamics on this shelf are undoubtedly affected by other factors, such as the across-shelf changes in sediment and bacterial community composition, grain size, and water circulation. Numerical hydrodynamic models indicate that under favorable wind conditions, numerical tracers introduced at the coast can move rapidly across the shelf to the reef proper (Luick et al., 2007). However, most tracers entering the GBR remain near the coast for most of the year, with residence times for conservative tracer particles ranging from 1 to 12 months, implying that any particles in the coastal water column will be transformed long before reaching the outer shelf, in some cases, recycled many times. Further, Uthicke and McGuire (2007) have found differences in the composition of bacterial communities between coastal and offshore sediments that may suggest differences in the relative importance of the various diagenetic pathways. For instance, the bacterial group representing most iron and manganese genotypes were not found in the offshore sediments and were rarely found in the coastal deposits. Despite differences in precipitation and total river discharge, there are very few differences between the far northern and northern regions in benthic biogeochemistry. Although there were higher percentages of total nitrogen input lost via denitrification in the far northern sector of the shelf than in the northern sector, these differences were not significant (ANOVA; \( P > 0.05 \)). The reasons for this difference are unknown, but may include differences in sediment oxygen penetration and the fact that, on average, sediments in the far northern sector had lower C:N ratios (12.5 vs. 29.5) and more N (0.05 vs. 0.03) than sediments in the northern sector. Not surprisingly, the overall average rates of sedimentation and mineralization, and C and N burial, were greater in the south reflecting higher rainfall and presumably greater rates of river discharge, resulting in a higher average rate of mineralization in the northern section (8883 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\)) than in the far north (7805 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\)). It is not possible to readily ascribe the regional differences to anthropogenic sources, although the catchments in the northern sector are much more heavily cultivated than those in the far north. Data from Low Isles taken in 1928–1929 (Marshall and Orr, 1931) suggest that sediments of the leeward side near where we sampled, were sandier. Whether or not this change toward muddier sediment is due to natural or anthropogenic change is problematical. Using the river export data of N and P from Furnas (2003) and making some conservative assumptions of shelf area over which this material deposits (1.0–1.5 × 10^9 m^2 in each section) terrestrial inputs equate to only a very small fraction (<10%) of nitrogen and phosphorus mineralization to these sediments. Benthic regeneration of NH_4^+ and PO_4^{3-} accounts for only 6–9% of the N requirements and 4–6% of the P requirements, for net phytoplankton production in these two sectors. These proportions are much less than the N (13%) and P (24%) requirements for phytoplankton productivity in the central section of the shelf (Alongi, 1989). Our denitrification rates are several times greater than the estimated N inputs from rivers in the far northern (40 mmol N m^{-2} y^{-1}) and northern (100 mmol N m^{-2} y^{-1}) GBR (Furnas, 2003). These estimates are crude, but suggest that other sources of organic matter are necessary to balance sedimentary C:N:P stoichiometry on the shelf. 5. Conclusions Most of the organic carbon and total nitrogen depositing to the shelf bed in the far northern and northern GBR was mineralized, with carbon and nitrogen burial being proportionally less on this shelf compared with other continental margins. Differences among locations in carbon and nitrogen flow related best to water depth and proximity to rivers, with higher rates of cycling in sediments closer to the coast. Sulfate reduction, on average, accounted for 30% of total carbon oxidation. The modest role of sulfate reduction was consistent with C:S ratios generally higher than that in other marine sediments. Discrepancies between \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) fluxes across the sediment–water interface and sediment incubations suggest that \( \approx 25\% \) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux was involved in the precipitation of carbonate minerals, especially in the subsurface deposits. Ammonification and nitrification rates were sufficiently high to support rapid rates of denitrification. Roughly 50% of total nitrogen input to the sediments was denitrified. Rapid rates of denitrification were likely fostered by suboxic and non-sulfidic conditions in these deposits, the low C:N ratio of depositing material, and intense bioturbation/disturbance of the surface sediment fabric. The average rates of sedimentation, mineralization, and burial of C and N were greater in the northern section of the shelf than in the far northern section, presumably due to higher rainfall and river discharge; phytoplankton production was similar between regions. Terrestrially derived material probably accounts only for about one-third or less of the observed mineralization rates, with inputs from other sources, such as neighboring reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, and shelf-edge upwelling, needed to balance the measured rates of recycling. Approximately 30–50% of plankton primary production was remineralized in the sediments, which is at the high end of the range found on other continental shelves, and reflected in the overall O_2:CO_2 flux ratio of 1.3. Rapid remineralization in these sediments is attributed to the deposition of high-quality organic material, the shallow nature of the shelf, warm year-round temperatures, and episodes of physical disturbance from cyclones and trawling. These factors foster physicochemical conditions favorable for maintaining rapid rates of microbial decomposition. The rapid and highly efficient recycling and retention of nutrients on the inner and middle shelf, often within coastal boundary layers, may help to explain why the outer shelf reefs remain relatively pristine. Deposition, mineralization, and storage of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern Great Barrier Reef shelf Daniel M. Alongi*, Lindsay A. Trott, John Pfitzner Australian Institute of Marine Science, PMB 3, Townsville MC, Qld. 4810, Australia Received 11 October 2006; received in revised form 10 July 2007; accepted 19 July 2007 Available online 1 August 2007 Abstract The flow of carbon and nitrogen in sediments of the far northern and northern sections of the Great Barrier Reef continental shelf was examined. Most of the organic carbon (81–94%) and total nitrogen (74–92%) depositing to the seabed was mineralized, with burial of carbon (6–19%) and nitrogen (8–20%) being proportionally less on this tropical shelf compared with other non-deltaic shelves. Differences in carbon and nitrogen mineralization among stations related best to water depth and proximity to river basins, with rates of mineralization based on net \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production ranging from 17 to 39 (mean = 23) mmol C m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\). The overall ratio of O\(_2\):CO\(_2\) flux was 1.3, close to the Redfield ratio, implying that most organic matter mineralized was algal. Sulfate reduction was estimated to account for \( \approx 30\% \) (range: 6–62%), and denitrification for \( \approx 5\% \) (range: 2–13%), of total C mineralization; there was no measurable CH\(_4\) production. Discrepancies between \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) production across the sediment–water interface and sediment incubations suggest that as much as 5 mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (\( \approx 25\% \) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux) was involved in carbonate mineral formation. Most microbial activity was in the upper 20 cm of sediment. Rates of net NH\(_4^+\) production ranged from 1.6 to 2.7 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\), with highly variable N\(_2\) fixation rates contributing little to total N input. Ammonification and nitrification rates were sufficient to support rapid rates of denitrification (range: 0.1–12.4 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)). On average, nearly 50% of total N input to the shelf sediment was denitrified. The average rates of sedimentation, mineralization, and burial of C and N were greater in the northern section of the shelf than in the far northern section, presumably due to higher rainfall and river discharge, as plankton production was similar between regions. The relative proportion of plankton primary production remineralized at the seafloor was in the range of 30–50% which is at the high end of the range found on other shelves. The highly reactive nature of these sediments is attributed to the deposition of high-quality organic material as well as to the shallowness of the shelf, warm temperatures year-round, and a variety of physical disturbances (cyclones, trawling) fostering physicochemical conditions favorable for maintaining rapid rates of microbial metabolism. The rapid and highly efficient recycling of nutrients on the inner and middle shelf may help to explain why the coral reefs on the outer shelf have remained unscathed from increased sediment delivery since European settlement. Introduction There is considerable concern about the impact and fate of terrestrially derived material entering the continental shelf of the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area (GBRWHA). Reduction in coral growth and a shift in the relative abundance and composition of corals and algae of nearshore fringing reefs, especially in inner shelf areas adjacent to intensively cultivated catchments, have been attributed to elevated availability of nutrients and suspended sediment loads (Fabricius et al., 2003). Intensification of land use and subsequent erosion of grazing land and crop land have resulted in an increase in sediment and nutrient delivery to the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) since the mid-1880s (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The magnitude of the increase is unclear, but more than one-half of sediment loading is estimated to come from grazing land, with 10% from crop land, and the remainder from natural erosion (Neil et al., 2002). Total sediment delivery is estimated at about 7 Mt y\(^{-1}\), with enhanced delivery possibly as high as 14–28 Mt y\(^{-1}\) (Neil et al., 2002; Furnas, 2003). The most intensive cultivation, and presumably the most intensive runoff, occurs in the latitudinal band of 16–18°S in the northern section of the GBRWHA. Less enhanced runoff occurs adjacent to less populated and cultivated catchments in the far northern section of the shelf. Nutrient cycling and inorganic and organic carbon dynamics is poorly understood on the GBR shelf, as most focus has been on cycling of elements on individual reefs rather than on non-reefal regions of the shelf. A number of studies have measured concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients along the length of the GBR, with data indicating concentrations typical of tropical waters under calm conditions, but elevated concentrations during periods of sustained winds when sediments are re-suspended, and during wet season plumes. GBR waters are characterized by N:P ratios of particulate matter of 8:1 and dissolved N:P ratios of 14:1 (Furnas, 2003). These low ratios likely reflect P adsorption onto inorganic particles, but may possibly indicate material of good nutritive value (Furnas et al., 1995). Sedimentation fluxes (based on data from sediment traps; Furnas et al., 1995) have been difficult to obtain in such shallow waters as most material recovered appears to be re-suspended matter, mucus, and other colloidal material. Stoichiometric ratios vary widely, but suggest fairly labile material settling to the seabed. Nutrient cycling in non-reefal GBR sediments is not well characterized, although several studies have pointed to \( \mu \)M concentrations of dissolved inorganic nutrients in interstitial water and rapid microbial activity (Alongi, 1989; Lourey et al., 2001). High rates of benthic microbial activity and lack of vertical profiles of dissolved and particulate nutrient concentrations suggest little burial of reactive organic matter, in agreement with low burial rates measured in the central GBR (Brunskill et al., 2002). The physical and biological complexity of the GBR limits the application of results from one section of the shelf to another. The GBR province is the exemplar of a carbonate rimmed shelf, and is one of the world’s largest continental margins with extensive mixed terrigenous–carbonate sedimentary facies (Hopley et al., 2007). The GBR shelf is a passive continental margin with a low seafloor gradient of <1:1000. The development and tectonic setting of this shelf is well understood compared with other tropical continental shelves. The shelf is wide (30–150 km) and shallow (<80 m at shelf break), encompassing an area of 225,000 km\(^2\), and is uniquely rimmed on the outer shelf margin by nearly 2500 individual coral reefs comprising the GBR, which stretches over 2000 km (10–24°S) parallel to the Queensland coast (Maxwell, 1968). The GBR shelf shares some characteristics with other tropical shelves, such as (1) a benthic fauna dominated by large epibenthos (e.g., echinoderms), lancelets, and large Foraminifera; (2) infaunal communities composed mostly of pioneering, small opportunists that surface deposit—and/or suspension feed; (3) abundant demersal assemblages, especially crustaceans; (4) intermittent intrusions of upwelled, nutrient-rich water; and (5) a summer wet season in which cyclones and monsoonal rains occur. The shallowness of the shelf in concert with severe summer weather, extensive trawling, and erratic nutrient inputs fosters plankton and benthic communities adapted to respond quickly to such disturbances and fluctuating rates of food supply. A sharp, across-shelf gradient of sedimentary facies from inshore terrigenous mud and quartz sand to mixed terrigenous–carbonate deposits mid-shelf to impure and pure carbonate within and between reefs on the outer margin is the dominant geological characteristic of the shelf (Hopley et al., 2007). In the far northern (Fig. 1a) and northern (Fig. 1b) sectors, this gradient narrows but persists from the south. On the inner shelf, the seaward limit Fig. 1. Depth contours are in meters. of the coastal zone is dynamic, varying in time and space and formed when turbid inshore and estuarine waters mix and are trapped along the coast; the coastal boundary breaks down under strong winds and river discharge (Wolanski and Ridd, 1990). River floods typically last for a few days and enter the shelf as plumes mostly in summer; runoff is negligible the rest of the year. Coastal boundary zones often form in bays sheltered by capes and headlands. Coastal waters move slowly longshore towards the headlands but may be periodically diverted as an ebb tidal jet peeling off from the headland, presumably enriching the middle shelf. Neither eddies formed by the rugged coastline nor longshore currents formed by the southeast trades can propagate in sheltered waters due to friction. Within the coastal boundary layer, dispersion of nutrients and particulate matter is by tidal diffusion only, especially when winds are light. It is for this reason that there is constant exchange between estuaries and the coastal boundary layer, but much slower rates of mixing between inshore and offshore waters (Wolanski, 1994). The phenomenon of trapping due to friction and the presence of coastal boundary zones ensure that most terrigenous sediment persists as a narrow band along the inner shelf. The regional distribution of Holocene terrigenous deposits and the sharp across-shelf gradient from terrigenous to carbonate facies have been well described (Maxwell, 1968; Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004; Hopley et al., 2007). Evidence from X-radiographs and radionuclide profiles shows that episodes of re-suspension, re-deposition, and intense reworking of surface deposits are common on the inner shelf (Alongi and Christoffersen, 1992; Brunskill et al., 2002). The sediment-starved middle shelf is a zone of transitional (30–60% carbonate) and impure (60–80% CaCO₃) carbonate facies. Surface water speeds commonly reach 50 cm s⁻¹ or more, but do not cause significant bedload transport. A recent analysis (Larcombe and Carter, 2004) has argued that cyclones transport post-storm mud drapes on top of the sandy middle shelf bed that are fully remixed into the sand facies by persistent bioturbation. Along shelf, cyclone-driven flow produces shelf-parallel, bed-sediment transport that is delimited as dunes, ribbons, or small dune areas on the middle shelf. Such strong flows (up to 130–200 cm s\(^{-1}\)) have resulted in erosion of Pleistocene deposits that are often exposed beneath a veneer of muddy sand and unconsolidated shell. This veneer, the net sedimentation of \( \approx 10,000 \) y of seabed exposure, is continually eroded and re-suspended by cyclones; mud in suspension is transported northwards along shelf and advected landwards. The result is dunes and ribbons of bioclastic deposits up to \( \approx 15 \) cm thick on the middle shelf (Belperio and Searle, 1988; Larcombe and Carter, 2004). It is on this portion of the shelf that epibenthic communities are most abundant and diverse, dominated by echinoderms, bryozoans, large ascidians, sponges, and Foraminifera (Alongi, 1989). In this paper, we detail studies of benthic metabolic rates and pathways of carbon and nitrogen cycling at inner and middle shelf sites proximal to impacted catchments on the northern GBR and to less heavily impacted catchments on the far northern GBR shelf. Some first-order calculations are also made to understand the benthic contribution to nutrient dynamics on these sections of the shelf and how (or if) they differ to earlier studies in the central section of the GBR shelf. 2.
