All data points represent mean (±1 SE) from season analysis under ambient nitrate concentrations (flux \( n = 6 \); organic matter content \( n = 3 \)). Note that values on the x-axis of A were inversed to present the relationship between N_2-N flux and the magnitude of nitrate uptake. Values on the y-axis of C were inversed to present the relationship between the magnitude of oxygen uptake and organic matter content. systems with limited nitrate supply (Burgin and Hamilton 2007; McCarthy and others 2007; Scott and others 2008). In addition to DNRA, assimilation by the microbial community could account for the surplus of nitrate entering the soil. Benthic microphytes are capable of high rates of nitrate uptake, even under dark conditions (Rysgaard and others 1993). Throughout our study, porewater salinities as well as hydrogen sulfide and ammonium concentrations were low and ammonium fluxes highly variable, indicating DNRA was not the dominant sink. The more probable nitrate sink was microbial assimilation. It is plausible that what appears to be excess nitrate taken up by the soil is an underestimate of denitrification due to nitrous oxide (N_2O) production or nitrogen fixation. Denitrification can end in either N_2O or N_2, with the relative proportion depending on soil conditions (Firestone and Tiedje 1979; Knowles 1982). In aquatic systems, nitrous oxide is often a small percent of the nitrogen gas evolved (<10%; Seitzinger and Nixon 1984; Seitzinger 1988; Silvennoinen and others 2008). And although the contribution of nitrous oxide in most coastal Louisiana wetlands exhibits a positive relationship with nitrate concentration (Smith and DeLaune 1983; Lindau and DeLaune 1991), Yu and others (2006) found nitrous oxide was still less than 2% of the nitrogen gas efflux from a coastal wetland receiving diverted Mississippi River water. Because the net N_2 flux as measured by N_2:Ar technique does not account for the production of nitrous oxide (Kana and others 1994), it is possible that nitrous oxide was a significant end-product of nitrate reduction and the denitrification rates presented here are underestimates. As previously mentioned, the N_2:Ar technique only provides an estimate of gross denitrification minus gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, the presence of nitrogen fixation could offset the 1:1 balance of nitrate (NO_3-N) reduced to N_2 (N_2-N) produced. In the spring, when nearly all the nitrate was removed from the overlying water (nitrate concentration: 2 μM), soils in the WLD switched from net denitrification (positive N_2 flux) to net nitrogen fixation (negative N_2 flux). Although it is possible that nitrogen fixation simply “turned on” in the absence of a reactive nitrogen source, the winter net N_2 flux at the Young site was also negative (net nitrogen fixation) under ambient nitrate concentrations of 94 μM. Thus, the disproportional amount of nitrate uptake to N_2 produced may not be the result of an additional nitrate sink, but evidence of nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is an energetically expensive process and the common paradigm, in aquatic systems, is that fixation only occurs when the availability of reactive nitrogen is low (Howarth and others 1988; Howarth and Marino 2006). However, appreciable rates of nitrogen fixation can occur even when reactive nitrogen is available (Gardner and others 2006; Fulweiler and others 2007; Scott and others 2008; Bertics and others 2010). Furthermore, studies measuring both denitrification and nitrogen fixation demonstrate that these processes can take place simultaneously in aquatic soils and sediments (Gardner and others 2006; Lee and Joye 2006; McCarthy and others 2007; Scott and others 2008). This study provides further evidence that both processes can occur contemporaneously in the presence of reactive nitrogen. Nutrient Biogeochemistry in Deltaic Floodplains Short-term patterns of nutrient accumulation along the 35-year WLD chronosequence were largely consistent with the early stages of soil development described for other types of ecosystems (Crews and others 1995; Wardle and others 2004; Selmants and Hart 2008, 2010). As soils developed in the deltaic floodplain, we observed a significant increase in the molar N:P ratio driven by the accumulation of nitrogen within the soil. Corresponding to the significant increase in soil nitrogen was a significant increase in organic matter (carbon) content. Increasing concentrations of nitrogen and organic matter during soil development have been documented in both natural (Tyler and Zieman 1999; Krull and Craft 2009) and created wetlands (Craft and others 1999, 2002; Anderson and others 2005; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The tight coupling between organic matter (carbon) and nitrogen is expected during wetland ecosystem succession as biological rather than geochemical processes control their accumulation (Craft 1997). In the WLD, the small, but significant increase in soil phosphorus with delta age represents a deviation from classic models of phosphorus dynamics (Walker and Syers 1976; Chapin and others 1994; Selmants and Hart 2010). At the Young site, total phosphorus content (per cm^3 soil) was approximately twofold to fivefold less than measured at the onset of soil development in terrestrial ecosystems and reflects the alluvial nature of substrate formation in the WLD (Chapin and others 1994; Crews and others 1995; Selmants and Hart 2010). However, despite the relatively low initial phosphorus content relative to other types of emerging landscapes, molar N:P ratios throughout the WLD were less than 16, indicating nitrogen limitation according to the Redfield ratio and a N:P ratio of 35 for wetland vegetation and soils (Redfield 1958; Bedford and others 1999). The slight increase observed in total phosphorus, the non-limiting nutrient, suggests that phosphorus dynamics during soil development in the WLD are independent of biological control and regulated by physical (for example, sediment trapping) or geochemical (for example, sorption) processes (Craft 1997; Megonigal and Neubauer 2009). In the present study, short-term patterns of phosphorus accumulation may be attributed to a difference in sediment grain size between the sites. A study conducted in the neighboring Atchafalaya delta observed an inverse relationship between total phosphorus and sediment grain size, with significantly higher phosphorus content in the suspended versus bedload sediment of the river (Poach and Faulkner 2007). Vegetation plays an important role in wetland sediment dynamics by decreasing flow velocities and trapping suspended sediments (Johnson and others 1985; Morris and others 2002). At the older sites, the year-round presence of aboveground vegetation, particularly during periods of high river flow, may capture a larger proportion of fine grain, phosphorus-rich sediments. Classic conceptual models of nutrient dynamics predict nitrogen fixation and atmospheric deposition to increase soil nitrogen content during early ecosystem development (Walker and Syers 1976; Gorham and others 1979; van Cleve and others 1991). Research in terrestrial ecosystems supports this prediction and shows the relative importance of nitrogen fixation to decrease with substrate age (Hobbie and others 1998; Pearson and Vitousek 2002; Schmidt and others 2008). Similarly, rates of nitrogen fixation tend to be greater in newly created or restored marshes relative to more mature wetland systems (Curin and others 1996; Piehler and others 1998; Tyler and others 2003). However, there is no evidence as to how the relationship between nitrogen fixation and substrate age may change under nitrate-enriched conditions. In the current study, net N_2 fluxes under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM) were largely positive. A positive net N_2 flux does not preclude the possibility of nitrogen fixation; it simply indicates greater rates of gross denitrification (direct denitrification + coupled nitrification–denitrification + anammox) than gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, under nitrate-enriched conditions, the dominant N_2 transformation (denitrification) was removing reactive nitrogen from the WLD, rather than increasing nitrogen via fixation as predicted by the classic conceptual models. Denitrification rates in newly created or restored marshes generally exhibit a positive relationship with wetland age (Thompson and others 1995; Currin and others 1996; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The low denitrification rates measured in the coarse soils of newly created wetlands have been attributed to a lack of organic matter and low moisture (Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). In addition, tidal flushing through these coarse, porous soils may increase porewater oxygen concentrations while simultaneously decreasing available nitrate, thereby decreasing denitrification rates (Thompson and others 1995). Various studies have reported a positive relationship between denitrification and soil organic matter content in wetland ecosystems (Davis and others 2004; Arango and others 2007; Dodla and others 2008; Hopfensperger and others 2009; Wolf and others 2011). Organic matter, specifically labile organic carbon compounds, can directly control the size or activity of the heterotrophic denitrifying population (Groffman 1994). In addition, organic matter can indirectly influence denitrification rates through regulation of soil metabolism, oxygen demand, and nitrogen remineralization (Seitzinger 1988; Cornwell and others 1999). During the winter and spring sampling events, net N_2 fluxes largely paralleled changes in organic matter, with significantly lower (or negative) fluxes occurring at the Young site (Figure 5). However, net N_2 fluxes in the summer/fall were similar across the delta and showed no correlation with organic matter. Summer/fall was the only season vegetation was present in all three sites. Previous studies show enhanced rates of denitrification in vegetated soils due to the leaching of labile organic carbon compounds from the roots of macrophytes and increased oxygen diffusion (via the coupled nitrification–denitrification pathway; Sherr and Payne 1978; Reddy and others 1989; Caffrey and Kemp 1992; Risgaard-Petersen and Jensen 1997). In the WLD, it appears as though the presence of vegetation, particularly in newly emerged substrates, may stimulate denitrification. This suggests that deltaic floodplains, at the mouth of major rivers, have a similar function along the longitudinal dimension of alluvial floodplains in reducing nitrate before river water enters coastal ocean. This function has two temporal dimensions that contribute to the fate of nitrate including age of the delta lobe and seasonal flood-pulse effects of vegetation and flooding frequency. CONCLUSIONS Overall, this study suggests that classic conceptual models of soil development should be applied with caution when describing short-term patterns of nutrient biogeochemistry during the early successional stages of the delta cycle. Throughout the 35-year WLD chronosequence, total nitrogen and organic matter (carbon) content exhibited a positive relationship with delta age similar to the general patterns previously described for both alluvial and terrestrial ecosystems. However, in contrast to these other ecosystems, the mechanisms controlling phosphorus dynamics yielded a slight increase in total phosphorus content as soils within the WLD developed. When using the alluvial floodplain model to predict net N_2 fluxes during delta development, the availability of nitrogen, specifically nitrate, as well as delta age needs to be taken into consideration. Under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM), the net exchange of N_2 gas was largely positive, indicating greater rates of gross denitrification than gross nitrogen fixation. In the absence of nitrate, the net N_2 flux reversed and soils exhibited net fixation. Soil organic matter content in conjunction with the presence of vegetation significantly affected net N_2, oxygen, nitrate, and nitrite fluxes yielding lower fluxes at the Young site (~10 years old). Consequently, as soils in the WLD age, their capacity for nitrate uptake and net denitrification increases. We conclude that early stages of delta development have significant capacity to remove nitrate from river waters as they are transported to nearshore waters. Thus, the formation of a river-dominated deltaic coast will reduce nutrient enrichment as organic matter content in soils increase with vegetative colonization of emerging landscapes. Nutrient Biogeochemistry During the Early Stages of Delta Development in the Mississippi River Deltaic Plain Kelly M. Henry* and Robert R. Twilley Department of Oceanography and Coastal Sciences, School of the Coast and Environment, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803, USA ABSTRACT Nutrient biogeochemistry associated with the early stages of soil development in deltaic floodplains has not been well defined. Such a model should follow classic patterns of soil nutrient pools described for alluvial ecosystems that are dominated by mineral matter high in phosphorus and low in carbon and nitrogen. A contrast with classic models of soil development is the anthropogenically enriched high nitrate conditions due to agricultural fertilization in upstream watersheds. Here we determine if short-term patterns of soil chemistry and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes along the emerging Wax Lake delta (WLD) chronosequence are consistent with conceptual models of long-term nutrient availability described for other ecosystems. We add a low nitrate treatment more typical of historic delta development to evaluate the role of nitrate enrichment in determining the net dinitrogen (N_2) flux. Throughout the 35-year chronosequence, soil nitrogen and organic matter content significantly increased by an order of magnitude, whereas phosphorus exhibited a less pronounced increase. Under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM), mean net N_2 fluxes (157.5 μmol N m^{-2} h^{-1}) indicated greater rates of gross denitrification than gross nitrogen fixation; however, under low nitrate concentrations (<2 μM), soils switched from net denitrification to net nitrogen fixation (−74.5 μmol N m^{-2} h^{-1}). As soils in the WLD aged, the subsequent increase in organic matter stimulated net N_2, oxygen, nitrate, and nitrite fluxes producing greater fluxes in more mature soils. In conclusion, soil nitrogen and carbon accumulation along an emerging delta chronosequence largely coincide with classic patterns of soil development described for alluvial floodplains, and substrate age together with ambient nitrogen availability can be used to predict net N_2 fluxes during early delta evolution. Key words: alluvial chronosequence; Atchafalaya basin; benthic fluxes; deltaic floodplain; N_2:Ar technique; nitrogen cycling. INTRODUCTION A Biogeochemical Model of Deltaic Floodplains Erosion of sediment from hillslopes and upland floodplains within major river basins produces mineral particles that are transported to the coast and deposited to form deltaic floodplains (Mulder and Syvitski 1996). Land created by this process supports the development of diverse wetland habitats that are associated with the early transgressiveional sequences of the delta cycle (Neill and Deegan 1986; Shaffer and others 1992). These ecological patterns of vegetation formation and distribution during the different stages of the delta cycle are well described for coastal alluvial systems (Boyd and Penland 1988; Keddy and others 2007). Surprisingly, there is a paucity of information specifying the biogeochemical patterns associated with delta formation and river abandonment in these depositional environments (hereafter referred to as deltaic floodplains). This geomorphic feature represents a part of the longitudinal continuum of riparian systems along major rivers from the upland watershed to the coast (Bayley 1995; Brown and others 1997; Noe and others 2013). The biogeochemistry of alluvial floodplains influences the fate of nitrogen and phosphorus determined by the inundation of river waters across the riparian landscapes during flood-pulse events (Junk and others 1989; Noe and others 2013). The basic longitudinal processing of nutrients at the mouth of major rivers is a missing component of understanding hydrologic connectivity and biogeochemical function in deltaic floodplains before river nutrients enter the coastal ocean. Biogeochemical patterns in deltaic floodplains should follow classic patterns of soil nutrient pools according to the conceptual model of emerging alluvial landscapes dominated by mineral matter and void of significant ecological feedback on organic matter development (van Cleve and others 1991; Brinson and others 1984; Olff and others 1997). A variety of models for soil development in emerging terrestrial landscapes describe nutrient accumulation after mud flows (Dickson and Crocker 1953), glacial recession (Crocker and Major 1955; Bormann and Sidle 1990), volcanic eruption (Vitousek and others 1983; Vitousek and Farrington 1997), and sand dune stabilization (Lichter 1998; Tackett and Craft 2010). In most models, young ecosystems tend to exhibit nitrogen limited plant growth (Vitousek and Howarth 1991; Vitousek and Farrington 1997) and support symbiotic nitrogen fixation (Hobbie and others 1998; Pearson and Vitousek 2002). As soils develop, they generally show a marked decrease in available phosphorus coupled to an increase in nitrogen (Bormann and Sidle 1990; Chapin and others 1994; Crews and others 1995; Hedin and others 2003). Coinciding with increased nitrogen availability are increased rates of nitrogen mineralization, nitrification, and nitrous oxide production (Riley and Vitousek 1995; Hedin and others 2003; Selmants and Hart 2008). With time, the increase in nitrogen shifts plant growth to phosphorus limitation (Chapin and others 1994; Vitousek and Farrington 1997; Wardle and others 2004). Alluvial soils in upland floodplains are distinct from the primary substrates described above with a higher potential for organic matter and nitrogen enrichment and the weathering of rock-derived minerals such as phosphorus (van Cleve and others 1991). Furthermore, fluvial systems are located at the interface of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, and as such, are noted biogeochemical hotspots for nutrient cycling within the landscape (McClain and others 2003; Burt and Pinay 2005). Nitrate Enrichment of Deltaic Floodplains Use of these classic alluvial and terrestrial models to explain biogeochemical patterns in recently exposed deltaic landscapes is complicated by the global imbalance of nitrogen in the environment. Human activity throughout the last century has exponentially increased biologically available nitrogen by doubling the rate at which reactive nitrogen is added to the biosphere (Vitousek and others 1997; Galloway and others 2004). The widespread use of industrial fertilizers in expanded agricultural production has altered the nitrogen chemistry of riverine and coastal waters. In the Mississippi River, concentrations of nitrate have tripled in the last four decades leading to enhanced productivity of coastal waters and causing an expanded hypoxic region along the Louisiana Bight (Goolsby and Battaglin 2001; Rabalais and others 2002; Broussard and Turner 2009). The elevated nitrate levels in the Mississippi River serve as an additional source of nitrogen in the early depositional landscapes of the deltaic floodplain and present an interesting perspective on the biogeochemical model of alluvial soil development. The classic models assume low nitrogen availability at the initiation of soil formation, while soils are slowly enriched with nitrogen via nitrogen fixation. Prior to the fertilization of the Mississippi River basin, this was the likely biogeochemical pattern during delta formation. However, the presence of high nitrate concentrations in the waters of the Mississippi River may reduce rates of nitrogen fixation relative to denitrification in the early successional stages of the delta. Yet, denitrification rates are dependent on the organic matter content of wetland soils (Davis and others 2004; Dodla and others 2008; Wolf and others 2011); and as a result, denitrification may remain limited in early depositional landscapes that lack organic matter to fuel this dissimilative process. Consequently, the biogeochemical model of deltaic floodplains may require some modification from observations made during soil development in ecosystems with low nitrogen inputs. Finally, the biogeochemical model associated with delta formation is important to understanding how these ecosystems reduce nitrogen loading to coastal and offshore environments. Present management of the lower Mississippi River basin is based on the mid-1800s decision to control floods and protect people using a continuous network of levees rather than a system of major outlets (Taylor 1904; Criss and Shock 2001). Today, the Mississippi River delta is losing extensive areas of wetland because sediment delivery to the coastal basins is restricted by levees that prevent flood pulses at high river stage (Fischetti 2001; Day and others 2007; Paola and others 2011). To increase wetland stability and mitigate further loss, large-scale restoration efforts have been proposed to divert freshwater and sediment from the Mississippi River back into coastal bay environments (Kim and others 2009; Paola and others 2011; Louisiana Coastal Master Plan 2012). These freshwater diversion projects are designed to reduce salinity and increase sediment delivery to the receiving basin by mimicking the overbank flooding that occurs during natural delta development (Twilley and Rivera-Monroy 2009; Paola and others 2011). There is a particular interest in the capacity of deltaic wetlands to remove the reactive nitrogen introduced by these diversions via the process of denitrification (Lindau and others 1988, 1994, 2008; DeLaune and Jugsujinda 2003, 2005). Ultimately, the ability of emerging wetlands to reduce the nitrate load in the Mississippi River depends on the development of biogeochemical cycles as sediment deposition from diversions forms alluvial substrates. The present study applies the alluvial floodplain model to describe patterns of nutrient biogeochemistry during the initial stages of delta formation using the Wax Lake delta (WLD), an emerging deltaic floodplain on the Louisiana coast. Our study determines if short-term patterns of soil chemistry and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes along an emerging delta chronosequence are consistent with the alluvial floodplain model of long-term nutrient availability during ecosystem development. Then, by contrasting the current anthropogenically enriched high nitrate scenario with a low nitrate scenario more typical of historic delta development, we evaluate the role of nitrate enrichment in determining the net N\(_2\) flux during the evolution of deltaic coasts. Finally, we assess the capacity of deltaic floodplains to reduce nitrogen load by denitrification. Our approach was to measure soil chemistry and net N\(_2\), oxygen, and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes to draw relationships between the early stages of soil development and nutrient biogeochemistry during the evolution of a deltaic floodplain. Wax Lake Delta as a Model Deltaic Floodplain Located within the Atchafalaya basin of the Mississippi River deltaic plain, the WLD provides an ideal ecosystem to develop a biogeochemical model of alluvial soil formation for a deltaic coast. The Atchafalaya River begins at the convergence of the Mississippi and the Red Rivers and flows approximately 275 km through the wooded lowland and cypress-tupelo swamps of the Atchafalaya basin before reaching the Gulf of Mexico. In 1942, the Wax Lake outlet was constructed off of the Atchafalaya River to provide flood relief for the lower Atchafalaya basin (Figure 1). At the convergence, the Old River Control Structure was completed in 1964 to stabilize the Atchafalaya River at 30% of the combined flows of the Mississippi and Red Rivers (long-term, mean annual discharge 6,400 m\(^3\) s\(^{-1}\); Lane and others 2011). Thirty percent of flow from the Atchafalaya River is diverted through the Wax Lake outlet, approximately 10% of the Mississippi River discharge. Two deltas are currently forming in Atchafalaya Bay, the Atchafalaya and the WLDs; however, only the WLD has been allowed to form naturally without any major human manipulation for navigational purposes (Roberts and others 1997; Allen and others 2012). The WLD first emerged above mean sea level after the unusually high spring flood of 1973 and has experienced rapid subaerial growth throughout the last 35 years (1 km\(^2\) y\(^{-1}\); Allen and others 2012). Because it is such a young delta, aerial photographs and satellite images allow for approximate aging of the delta lobes (Wellner and others 2006). Using distance from the head of the WLD as a proxy for substrate age, three sites were established on lobes 1.0, 4.5, and 7.5 km from the head of the delta (Figure 1). Based on aerial photographs from Wellner and others (2006), the approximate ages of the corresponding alluvial substrates are 35, 23, and 10 years old, respectively. These delta lobes differ markedly in substrate age, elevation, and plant community, but share similar parent material, river hydrology, and climate. Figure 1. Location of the age gradient of study sites across the WLD, Louisiana. The 35-year old site is closest to the head of the delta and the Wax Lake outlet (Wellner and others 2006). The 10-year old site is closest to the Gulf of Mexico (Wellner and others 2006). Image courtesy of United States Geological Survey. Vegetation at the Young site (~10 years; 29°30′06″N, 091°28′46″W) is dominated by Sagittaria platyphylla. The Intermediate site (~23 years; 29°30′45″N, 091°27′56″W) contains a mixed community composed of Colocasia esculenta, Phragmites australis, Polygonum punctatum, Typha spp., Schoenoplectus spp., and Zizaniopsis miliacea. Salix nigra is the dominant vegetation present at the Older site (~35 years; 29°31′56″N, 091°26′10″W), with an understory of C. esculenta and P. punctatum. Herbaceous wetland species, such as C. esculenta, P. punctatum, and S. platyphylla, exhibit senescence in the fall and winter, with aboveground growth occurring during the spring and summer. Thus, aboveground vegetation is completely absent from the Young site and largely reduced at the Intermediate site during the winter and early spring months. Sediments throughout the sedimentary framework of the WLD increase in coarseness toward the surface facies and contain a high percentage of medium to fine sand and coarse silt (Roberts and others 1997). Water level in the WLD is influenced by diurnal microtides (0.3 m), seasonal wind-driven events, and the annual flood cycle of the Atchafalaya River (Swenson and Sasser 1992; Holm and Sasser 2001). The combination of these hydrological forcing factors causes water levels to rise through the winter, peak in the spring, and decrease to a minimum in the fall (Swenson and Sasser 1992; NOAA Tides and Currents 2012). Climate in the region is humid subtropical (Peel and others 2007) and characterized by mild winters (6°C), hot summers (30°C), and ample rainfall (160 cm y\(^{-1}\); National Climatic Data Center 2012). MATERIALS AND METHODS Soil and Porewater Surveys In August 2010, we established an 8 km transect from the head of the WLD to the Gulf of Mexico. Triplicate soil cores (10 cm internal diameter by 10 cm depth) were collected at 1.0, 4.5, and 7.5 km to capture soil conditions across the age gradient of the WLD (Figure 1). These three sampling locations correspond to the Older (~35 years), Intermediate (~23 years), and Young (~10 years) sites, respectively. The top 4 cm of soil, including roots, rhizomes, and organisms, were oven-dried at 60°C to a constant weight and bulk density was determined Table 1. Each sample was ground to 250 μm in a Wiley Mill and total organic matter was determined by loss on ignition at 550°C for 2 h (Davies 1974). Total carbon and nitrogen were determined with an ECS 4010 elemental analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies, Inc., Valencia, California). After combustion in a furnace for 2 h at 550°C, total phosphorus was extracted from soil samples with 1 M HCl (Aspila and others 1976) and determined by colorimetric analysis using a Flow Solution IV autoanalyzer (OI Analytical, College Station, Texas). In late summer/early fall (September 2010), winter (January 2011), and spring (May 2011), triplicate 90 ml samples of porewater were collected from a depth of 10 cm within the Young, Intermediate, and Older sites. Porewater samples were collected by inserting rigid aquarium tubing affixed to a 60 ml syringe into the soil and using suction to draw water from the pore spaces between the soil particles (Hargis and Twilley 1994). Temperature, salinity, and pH, as well as hydrogen sulfide (H2S), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and dissolved inorganic nutrient [nitrite (NO2−), nitrate (NO3−), ammonium (NH4+), and phosphate (PO43−)] concentrations were determined according to standard analytical methods (Supplementary Material). Soil oxidation–reduction (redox) potential was measured at 10 cm with a platinum electrode (Hargis and Twilley 1994). Soil–water Column Flux Experiments During each season, triplicate, intact soil cores (10 cm internal diameter by 10 cm depth) were collected from each site for soil–water column flux experiments. Care was taken to avoid aboveground vegetation; yet roots, rhizomes, and an occasional small plant were captured within the cores. After collection, soil cores were placed in a cooler and transported to an environmental growth chamber at Louisiana State University. Cores were pre-incubated in a water bath for 24–48 h with air gently bubbling through the overlying water. During the pre-incubation period, chamber conditions were maintained at ambient field temperature (25°C in summer/fall and spring, and 12°C in winter) and in continuous darkness. Surface water was collected from the Wax Lake outlet (hereafter referred to as site water) and filtered immediately to 0.2 μm. Site water was stored in the dark, at ambient field temperature. In winter (February 2011) and spring (June 2011), three additional soil cores (10 cm internal diameter by 10 cm depth) were collected from each site for determination of microbial biomass carbon and chlorophyll a and analyzed according to standard analytical methods (Supplementary Material). A total of five experiments were completed to capture seasonal variability in net N2, oxygen, and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes and to evaluate the importance of nitrate enrichment in determining the net N2 flux (Table 1). During each season (summer/fall, winter, and spring), soil cores from the three sites were incubated with the filtered site water containing ambient field nitrate concentrations (see Table 1 for the season-specific ambient nitrate concentrations). These three experiments are hereafter referred to as the seasonal experiments. Then in winter and spring, two additional experiments were conducted on the same soil cores, using modified site water, with reduced nitrate concentrations. These two experiments are hereafter referred to as the low nitrate experiments. By passing the filtered site water through a glass column packed with a nitrate-specific resin (ResinTech SIR-100-HP, West Berlin, New Jersey), we decreased the nitrate concentration in a subsample of the site water to 10 μM in the winter and 2 μM in the spring. After the seasonal experiment, the same cores were pre-incubated for 24–48 h with the low nitrate site water. Once the pre-incubation was complete, the soil cores were incubated using the low nitrate site water. During each of the five experiments (three seasonal and two low nitrate), two separate incubations were conducted. The first incubation collected water samples for dissolve gas analysis (N_2 and O_2; gas incubation), and the second incubation collected water samples for dissolved inorganic nutrient analysis (NO_2^−, NO_3^−, NH_4^+, and PO_4^{−3}; nutrient incubation). Temperature, salinity, nitrate concentrations, and light conditions were identical between the gas and nutrient incubations (Table 1). Before beginning the gas incubation, we carefully replaced the overlying water in all the cores with filtered site water and then sealed the cores with a gas-tight lid. Magnetic stir bars affixed to each lid gently mixed (~55 rpm) the overlying water throughout the incubation. Cores were incubated in the dark for 3–10 h, followed by 4–13 h of light (~300 μmol m^{-2} s^{-1}). The transition from dark to light conditions occurred after a 2 ppm decrease in dissolved oxygen (Giblin and others 1997; Fulweiler and others 2008) and the total incubation time depended on the ambient water temperature (Table 1). Cores remained sealed during the transition from dark to light conditions and overlying water was not replaced (Eyre and Ferguson 2002). Replicate water samples for N_2 analysis were collected ten times evenly spaced throughout the incubation (five samples in the dark and light, respectively). These samples were collected into 12 ml exetainers (Labco Limited, High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, England) and preserved with 250 μl ZnCl_2 (50% w/v; Nielsen and Glud 1996). Dissolved oxygen concentrations were measured four times evenly spaced throughout the incubation (two samples in the dark and light, respectively). These measurements were made with a Hach LDO101-01 dissolved oxygen probe. After completing the gas incubation, the overlying water was replaced and the nutrient incubation commenced. Water samples were collected and filtered with a Cole-Parmer RC-membrane filter (0.45 μm) for dissolved inorganic nutrients (NO_2^−, NO_3^−, NH_4^+, and PO_4^{−3}) at approximately the same ten sampling intervals. Once the gas and nutrient incubations were complete, the top 4 cm of soil was collected from each core, oven-dried at 60°C, and analyzed for total organic matter, carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus content (soil nutrient analysis described above). Dissolved Gas and Inorganic Nutrient Analysis Dinitrogen concentrations were determined by the N_2:Ar technique using a Pfeiffer Prisma QME 200 quadrupole mass spectrometer (Bay Instruments, Easton, Maryland) equipped with a flow-through silicone capillary membrane inlet (MIMS; Kana and others 1994). The MIMS was modified with a copper reduction column and furnace heated to 600°C to remove oxygen from the dissolved gas samples, thereby eliminating the potential for an oxygen effect on N_2 measurements and subsequently increasing sample precision to ±0.01% (Eyre and others 2002). Dinitrogen concentrations were determined for each sample by multiplying the N_2:Ar ratio by the Ar concentration at air saturation (Colt 1984). Filtered porewater and nutrient incubation water samples were analyzed colorimetrically for NO_2^−, NO_3^−, NH_4^+, and PO_4^{−3} using a Flow IV OI analytical autoanalyzer (Strickland and Parsons 1972; Parsons and others 1984). Dinitrogen and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes across the soil–water interface were calculated from the slope of a five-point linear regression of concentration as a function of time. To calculate the flux, the slope was multiplied by the headspace water volume and then divided by the core surface area. Prior to fitting each five-point linear regression, data were checked for outliers and evidence of experimental artifacts. If the relationship between analyte concentration and time was nonlinear (\( P > 0.1 \)), the slope and subsequently the flux were considered zero. Negative fluxes denote soil consumption or uptake, whereas positive fluxes denote soil production or release. The N_2:Ar ratio is a measure of the net N_2 flux (gross denitrification–gross nitrogen fixation); therefore, a positive flux equals net denitrification, whereas a negative flux equals net nitrogen fixation. One limitation of the N_2:Ar technique is the inability to differentiate between N_2 production pathways (for example, direct denitrification, coupled nitrification–denitrification, and anammox) (Groffman and others 2006; Fulweiler and others 2008). Statistical Analysis The relationship between distance from the head of the WLD (used as a proxy for delta age) and soil organic matter and nutrient content were described with a series of simple linear regressions. Soil microbial biomass carbon and chlorophyll \( a \) data were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with repeated measures to test for differences among sites (Young, Intermediate, and Older) and between seasons (winter and spring). Porewater chemistry and soil redox data were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA with repeated measures to test for differences among sites (Young, Intermediate, and Older) and seasons (summer/fall, winter, and spring). The dissolved gas and inorganic nutrient flux data were divided into two separate analyses. The first analysis only included data from the seasonal experiments and will be referred to as the season analysis. This analysis tested for significant differences among sites (Young, Intermediate, and Older) and seasons (summer/fall, winter, and spring), and between light conditions (dark and light) using a three-way ANOVA with repeated measures. The second analysis only included the two seasons we conducted experiments under ambient and low nitrate conditions and will be referred to as the low nitrate analysis. The low nitrate analysis tested for significant differences among sites (Young, Intermediate, and Older), and between seasons (winter and spring), nitrate concentrations (ambient and low), and light conditions (dark and light) using a four-way ANOVA with repeated measures. For all analyses, site, season, nitrate concentration, and light condition were considered fixed effects. Interaction effects were considered for all analyses and pairwise comparisons among treatments were described with a Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test. Statistical analyses were performed with SAS PROC MIXED and significance was assessed at the 0.05 level (SAS Institute 2012). RESULTS Soil and Porewater Properties Both total phosphorus and nitrogen in the top 4 cm of soil exhibited a significant, positive relationship with delta age and simple linear regression explained 42 and 76% of the variability in the data, respectively (Figure 2A). Total phosphorus increased from 0.04 to 0.07% and total nitrogen increased from 0.06 to 0.56% along the age gradient of the WLD. The molar nitrogen to phosphorus (N:P) ratio was positively correlated with delta age and increased from 3.6 at the Young site (~10 years) to 15.6 at the Older site (~35 years; Figure 2B). Organic matter content ranged from 2.8% at the Young site to 18.2% at the Older site and exhibited a significant, positive relationship with delta age (Figure 2C). There was no relationship between the molar carbon to nitrogen (C:N) ratio and delta age (mean 13.2; Figure 2B). Soil chlorophyll \( a \), redox, and pore-water chemistry were variable, with no consistent trends among the sites and seasons (Table S2). Seasonal Flux Experiments Initial nitrate concentrations in the water overlying the soil cores were 75, 94, and 62 \( \mu \)M for the summer/fall, winter, and spring incubations, respectively (Table 1). Net \( N_2 \) fluxes across the soil–water interface were largely positive indicating net denitrification (mean \( 157.5 \) \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)). We observed no significant difference in net \( N_2 \) flux between sites during the summer/fall sampling event (Figure 3A). However, in the winter and spring, net \( N_2 \) fluxes at the Young site were significantly lower than fluxes at the Older site. Oxygen fluxes were dominated by soil consumption (mean \( -69.1 \) mg O\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)), and within each season, soil oxygen demand was 36–83% lower at the Young site (Figure 3B). DISCUSSION The Role of Nitrate Enrichment in Determining Net N_2 Fluxes Canonical denitrification in wetland soils and sediments can be fueled by nitrate diffusing from the water column (direct denitrification), nitrate formed within the soil during the oxidation of ammonium (coupled nitrification–denitrification), or nitrate advected from groundwater (Seitzinger 1988; Groffman 1994; Hopkinson and Giblin 2008). In coastal environments, nitrate availability often limits rates of direct denitrification; and as a result, coupled nitrification–denitrification is the dominant N_2 production pathway (Giblin and others 2010; Hamersley and Howes 2003; Poulin and others 2007). However, in the WLD, net N_2 production was highly correlated to nitrate uptake, under ambient nitrate concentrations (\( r^2 = 0.75 \); Figure 5). This suggests that the production of N_2 gas was primarily via direct denitrification and the contribution of coupled nitrification–denitrification to the net N_2 flux was relatively insignificant. A closer look at the relationship between nitrate uptake and net N_2 production reveals that for every 1 mol of NO_3^-N entering the soil only 0.28 mol of N_2-N were released. This begs the question, where did the excess nitrate go? In addition to denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) and microbial assimilation serve as sinks for nitrate. A number of studies provide evidence that DNRA is a significant nitrate reduction pathway in freshwater and marine ecosystems (An and Gardner 2002; Gardner and others 2006; Scott and others 2008; Giblin and others 2010). Increasing salinities and corresponding sulfide concentrations can enhance rates of chemolithoautotrophic DNRA by inhibiting denitrification and providing an electron donor for DNRA (An and Gardner 2002; Burgin and Hamilton 2007; Giblin and others 2010). Organic matter loading can increase rates of fermentative DNRA, particularly in ![Three scatter plots showing relationships between N2-N flux, NO3^- flux, and organic matter content.](page_1042_180_484_1202.png) Figure 5. Values on the y-axis of C were inversed to present the relationship between the magnitude of oxygen uptake and organic matter content. systems with limited nitrate supply (Burgin and Hamilton 2007; McCarthy and others 2007; Scott and others 2008). In addition to DNRA, assimilation by the microbial community could account for the surplus of nitrate entering the soil. Benthic microphytes are capable of high rates of nitrate uptake, even under dark conditions (Rysgaard and others 1993). Throughout our study, porewater salinities as well as hydrogen sulfide and ammonium concentrations were low and ammonium fluxes highly variable, indicating DNRA was not the dominant sink. The more probable nitrate sink was microbial assimilation. It is plausible that what appears to be excess nitrate taken up by the soil is an underestimate of denitrification due to nitrous oxide (N_2O) production or nitrogen fixation. Denitrification can end in either N_2O or N_2, with the relative proportion depending on soil conditions (Firestone and Tiedje 1979; Knowles 1982). In aquatic systems, nitrous oxide is often a small percent of the nitrogen gas evolved (<10%; Seitzinger and Nixon 1984; Seitzinger 1988; Silvennoinen and others 2008). And although the contribution of nitrous oxide in most coastal Louisiana wetlands exhibits a positive relationship with nitrate concentration (Smith and DeLaune 1983; Lindau and DeLaune 1991), Yu and others (2006) found nitrous oxide was still less than 2% of the nitrogen gas efflux from a coastal wetland receiving diverted Mississippi River water. Because the net N_2 flux as measured by N_2:Ar technique does not account for the production of nitrous oxide (Kana and others 1994), it is possible that nitrous oxide was a significant end-product of nitrate reduction and the denitrification rates presented here are underestimates. As previously mentioned, the N_2:Ar technique only provides an estimate of gross denitrification minus gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, the presence of nitrogen fixation could offset the 1:1 balance of nitrate (NO_3-N) reduced to N_2 (N_2-N) produced. In the spring, when nearly all the nitrate was removed from the overlying water (nitrate concentration: 2 μM), soils in the WLD switched from net denitrification (positive N_2 flux) to net nitrogen fixation (negative N_2 flux). Although it is possible that nitrogen fixation simply “turned on” in the absence of a reactive nitrogen source, the winter net N_2 flux at the Young site was also negative (net nitrogen fixation) under ambient nitrate concentrations of 94 μM. Thus, the disproportional amount of nitrate uptake to N_2 produced may not be the result of an additional nitrate sink, but evidence of nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is an energetically expensive process and the common paradigm, in aquatic systems, is that fixation only occurs when the availability of reactive nitrogen is low (Howarth and others 1988; Howarth and Marino 2006). However, appreciable rates of nitrogen fixation can occur even when reactive nitrogen is available (Gardner and others 2006; Fulweiler and others 2007; Scott and others 2008; Bertics and others 2010). Furthermore, studies measuring both denitrification and nitrogen fixation demonstrate that these processes can take place simultaneously in aquatic soils and sediments (Gardner and others 2006; Lee and Joye 2006; McCarthy and others 2007; Scott and others 2008). This study provides further evidence that both processes can occur contemporaneously in the presence of reactive nitrogen. Nutrient Biogeochemistry in Deltaic Floodplains Short-term patterns of nutrient accumulation along the 35-year WLD chronosequence were largely consistent with the early stages of soil development described for other types of ecosystems (Crews and others 1995; Wardle and others 2004; Selmants and Hart 2008, 2010). As soils developed in the deltaic floodplain, we observed a significant increase in the molar N:P ratio driven by the accumulation of nitrogen within the soil. Corresponding to the significant increase in soil nitrogen was a significant increase in organic matter (carbon) content. Increasing concentrations of nitrogen and organic matter during soil development have been documented in both natural (Tyler and Zieman 1999; Krull and Craft 2009) and created wetlands (Craft and others 1999, 2002; Anderson and others 2005; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The tight coupling between organic matter (carbon) and nitrogen is expected during wetland ecosystem succession as biological rather than geochemical processes control their accumulation (Craft 1997). In the WLD, the small, but significant increase in soil phosphorus with delta age represents a deviation from classic models of phosphorus dynamics (Walker and Syers 1976; Chapin and others 1994; Selmants and Hart 2010). At the Young site, total phosphorus content (per cm^3 soil) was approximately twofold to fivefold less than measured at the onset of soil development in terrestrial ecosystems and reflects the alluvial nature of substrate formation in the WLD (Chapin and others 1994; Crews and others 1995; Selmants and Hart 2010). However, despite the relatively low initial phosphorus content relative to other types of emerging landscapes, molar N:P ratios throughout the WLD were less than 16, indicating nitrogen limitation according to the Redfield ratio and a N:P ratio of 35 for wetland vegetation and soils (Redfield 1958; Bedford and others 1999). The slight increase observed in total phosphorus, the non-limiting nutrient, suggests that phosphorus dynamics during soil development in the WLD are independent of biological control and regulated by physical (for example, sediment trapping) or geochemical (for example, sorption) processes (Craft 1997; Megonigal and Neubauer 2009). In the present study, short-term patterns of phosphorus accumulation may be attributed to a difference in sediment grain size between the sites. A study conducted in the neighboring Atchafalaya delta observed an inverse relationship between total phosphorus and sediment grain size, with significantly higher phosphorus content in the suspended versus bedload sediment of the river (Poach and Faulkner 2007). Vegetation plays an important role in wetland sediment dynamics by decreasing flow velocities and trapping suspended sediments (Johnson and others 1985; Morris and others 2002). At the older sites, the year-round presence of aboveground vegetation, particularly during periods of high river flow, may capture a larger proportion of fine grain, phosphorus-rich sediments. Classic conceptual models of nutrient dynamics predict nitrogen fixation and atmospheric deposition to increase soil nitrogen content during early ecosystem development (Walker and Syers 1976; Gorham and others 1979; van Cleve and others 1991). Research in terrestrial ecosystems supports this prediction and shows the relative importance of nitrogen fixation to decrease with substrate age (Hobbie and others 1998; Pearson and Vitousek 2002; Schmidt and others 2008). Similarly, rates of nitrogen fixation tend to be greater in newly created or restored marshes relative to more mature wetland systems (Curin and others 1996; Piehler and others 1998; Tyler and others 2003). However, there is no evidence as to how the relationship between nitrogen fixation and substrate age may change under nitrate-enriched conditions. In the current study, net N_2 fluxes under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM) were largely positive. A positive net N_2 flux does not preclude the possibility of nitrogen fixation; it simply indicates greater rates of gross denitrification (direct denitrification + coupled nitrification–denitrification + anammox) than gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, under nitrate-enriched conditions, the dominant N_2 transformation (denitrification) was removing reactive nitrogen from the WLD, rather than increasing nitrogen via fixation as predicted by the classic conceptual models. Denitrification rates in newly created or restored marshes generally exhibit a positive relationship with wetland age (Thompson and others 1995; Currin and others 1996; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The low denitrification rates measured in the coarse soils of newly created wetlands have been attributed to a lack of organic matter and low moisture (Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). In addition, tidal flushing through these coarse, porous soils may increase porewater oxygen concentrations while simultaneously decreasing available nitrate, thereby decreasing denitrification rates (Thompson and others 1995). Various studies have reported a positive relationship between denitrification and soil organic matter content in wetland ecosystems (Davis and others 2004; Arango and others 2007; Dodla and others 2008; Hopfensperger and others 2009; Wolf and others 2011). Organic matter, specifically labile organic carbon compounds, can directly control the size or activity of the heterotrophic denitrifying population (Groffman 1994). In addition, organic matter can indirectly influence denitrification rates through regulation of soil metabolism, oxygen demand, and nitrogen remineralization (Seitzinger 1988; Cornwell and others 1999). During the winter and spring sampling events, net N_2 fluxes largely paralleled changes in organic matter, with significantly lower (or negative) fluxes occurring at the Young site (Figure 5). However, net N_2 fluxes in the summer/fall were similar across the delta and showed no correlation with organic matter. Summer/fall was the only season vegetation was present in all three sites. Previous studies show enhanced rates of denitrification in vegetated soils due to the leaching of labile organic carbon compounds from the roots of macrophytes and increased oxygen diffusion (via the coupled nitrification–denitrification pathway; Sherr and Payne 1978; Reddy and others 1989; Caffrey and Kemp 1992; Risgaard-Petersen and Jensen 1997). In the WLD, it appears as though the presence of vegetation, particularly in newly emerged substrates, may stimulate denitrification. This suggests that deltaic floodplains, at the mouth of major rivers, have a similar function along the longitudinal dimension of alluvial floodplains in reducing nitrate before river water enters coastal ocean. This function has two temporal dimensions that contribute to the fate of nitrate including age of the delta lobe and seasonal flood-pulse effects of vegetation and flooding frequency. CONCLUSIONS Overall, this study suggests that classic conceptual models of soil development should be applied with caution when describing short-term patterns of nutrient biogeochemistry during the early successional stages of the delta cycle. Throughout the 35-year WLD chronosequence, total nitrogen and organic matter (carbon) content exhibited a positive relationship with delta age similar to the general patterns previously described for both alluvial and terrestrial ecosystems. However, in contrast to these other ecosystems, the mechanisms controlling phosphorus dynamics yielded a slight increase in total phosphorus content as soils within the WLD developed. When using the alluvial floodplain model to predict net N_2 fluxes during delta development, the availability of nitrogen, specifically nitrate, as well as delta age needs to be taken into consideration. Under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM), the net exchange of N_2 gas was largely positive, indicating greater rates of gross denitrification than gross nitrogen fixation. In the absence of nitrate, the net N_2 flux reversed and soils exhibited net fixation. Soil organic matter content in conjunction with the presence of vegetation significantly affected net N_2, oxygen, nitrate, and nitrite fluxes yielding lower fluxes at the Young site (~10 years old). Consequently, as soils in the WLD age, their capacity for nitrate uptake and net denitrification increases. We conclude that early stages of delta development have significant capacity to remove nitrate from river waters as they are transported to nearshore waters. Thus, the formation of a river-dominated deltaic coast will reduce nutrient enrichment as organic matter content in soils increase with vegetative colonization of emerging landscapes.
